title: Investing Basics
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Discover what stocks, bonds, and index funds are, why investing is long-term, and how risk and reward go together.

questions.q: What does it mean to invest?
options: To put money into something hoping it grows in value over time
To hide cash in a drawer
To lend money and never expect it back
questions.explain: Investing aims to grow money over years by owning things like stocks or funds. It carries risk, unlike insured savings.

questions.q: What is a stock?
options: A small piece of ownership in a company
questions.explain: Buying a stock makes you a part owner of that company. Its value rises and falls with the company and the market.

questions.q: What is a bond?
options: A loan you make to a company or government that pays you interest
A savings certificate you cannot sell
questions.explain: Bond buyers lend money and receive interest payments plus their principal back later. Bonds are usually steadier than stocks but grow more slowly.

questions.q: What is diversification?
options: Putting all money into one stock
Spreading money across different investments so one loss hurts less
questions.explain: Diversification lowers risk because different investments do not all fall at once. It is the idea of not putting all eggs in one basket.

questions.q: What is an index fund?
options: A fund that owns many stocks at once to match a market index
A single stock picked by an expert
A bank account with a fixed rate
A list of companies on paper only
questions.explain: Index funds hold hundreds of companies in one purchase, giving instant diversification. They are a common beginner-friendly choice.

questions.q: Why do long time horizons help investors?
options: Prices can only go up over time
Short-term ups and downs matter less when money stays invested for years
Banks add secret bonuses after ten years
questions.explain: Markets swing in the short run but have historically recovered over long periods. Time does not remove risk, it just smooths the ride.

questions.q: Nia invests 1,000 dollars and it grows 10 percent in a year. How much is it worth before any fees or taxes?
questions.explain: Ten percent of 1,000 is 100, so the value becomes 1,100 dollars. Gains are never guaranteed and values can also fall.

questions.q: What is the relationship between risk and possible reward in investing?
options: More risk always means guaranteed profit
Risk and reward are never related
Safe investments always pay the most
Higher possible rewards usually come with higher risk of loss
questions.explain: Investments promising big returns can also lose big. Match your risk level to your goals and timeline.

questions.q: A friend guarantees an investment will double your money in one month with no risk. What should you think?
options: That is a major warning sign of a scam
It sounds like a normal index fund
Only banks can offer that deal
questions.explain: No legitimate investment guarantees high returns with no risk. Guaranteed quick riches is one of the most common scam signals.

questions.q: What is the best first investing step for most teens with a job?
options: Borrow money to buy one hot stock
Build a small emergency fund, then invest small amounts regularly for the long term
Put rent money into crypto this week
questions.explain: A safety cushion comes before investing so surprises never force you to sell. Then small, steady, diversified investing builds the habit.

title: Insurance Essentials
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Learn how insurance shares risk, what premiums and deductibles mean, and which kinds of coverage protect people every day.

questions.q: What is the basic idea of insurance?
options: One person pays for everyone else
Many people pay into a pool that helps the few who face a big loss
A savings account that doubles yearly
A way to avoid all accidents
questions.explain: Insurance spreads risk across many customers so one emergency does not ruin one family. The company pays covered claims from the pool.

questions.q: What is an insurance premium?
options: The amount the insurer pays you after a claim
A one-time fee for a drivers license
The regular payment you make to keep your coverage active
The total value of your car
questions.explain: Premiums are usually paid monthly or yearly to keep a policy active. Missing payments can cancel your coverage.

questions.q: What is a deductible?
options: The full cost of every repair
A discount the insurer gives you
The amount you pay yourself before insurance starts paying
questions.explain: If your deductible is 500 dollars, you pay the first 500 dollars of a covered loss. Higher deductibles usually mean lower premiums.

questions.q: Your car repair after a covered accident costs 1,800 dollars and your deductible is 500 dollars. How much does insurance pay?
questions.explain: Subtract your deductible from the cost: 1,800 minus 500 equals 1,300 dollars paid by insurance. You pay the 500 dollar deductible.

questions.q: Which type of insurance helps pay medical bills?
questions.explain: Health insurance helps cover doctor visits, hospital care, and prescriptions. Most states also require auto insurance for drivers.

questions.q: Why do states require drivers to carry auto liability insurance?
options: So a driver who causes a crash can help pay for others injuries and damage
questions.explain: Liability coverage protects other people from costs you cause. Driving uninsured can bring fines and personal debt.

questions.q: What does renters insurance typically cover?
options: Your belongings inside a rented home if they are stolen or damaged
questions.explain: Renters insurance is usually inexpensive and protects your clothes, electronics, and furniture. It often includes liability coverage too.

questions.q: Which choice would usually lower an auto insurance premium?
options: Choosing a higher deductible and keeping a clean driving record
Letting coverage lapse for a month
questions.explain: Insurers charge less when you take on more of the risk with a higher deductible and drive safely. Tickets and crashes raise premiums.

questions.q: A phone costs 800 dollars. A protection plan costs 15 dollars a month for 2 years, which totals 360 dollars, plus a 99 dollar claim fee. What is the total cost if you file one claim?
questions.explain: Add 360 plus 99 to get 459 dollars, more than half the phone price. Doing this math helps you judge whether a plan is worth it.

questions.q: When is buying insurance a smart move?
options: When the item is cheap and easy to replace
When a salesperson pressures you for one minute only
When a loss would be too big to pay for on your own
When you do not understand the policy at all
questions.explain: Insurance is for losses that would seriously hurt your finances, like a hospital stay or a totaled car. Small, affordable losses are often cheaper to self-cover.

title: Scams, Fraud and Future Planning
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Spot phishing, fake deals, and identity theft warning signs, then set goals and a simple plan that turns todays habits into future security.

questions.q: What is phishing?
options: A fake message that tries to trick you into sharing passwords or personal data
A safe way to reset passwords
questions.explain: Phishing messages copy real companies to steal logins and card numbers. Always reach the company through its official app or site, not the message link.

questions.q: A text says your bank account is locked and asks you to tap a link and enter your password within one hour. What is the safest response?
options: Tap quickly before time runs out
Reply with your password to prove it is you
Forward the text to friends to warn them by tapping the link
Do not tap the link; contact the bank through its official app or the number on your card
questions.explain: Urgency and surprise links are classic scam tools. Going directly to the official source lets you check safely.

questions.q: What is identity theft?
options: When someone uses your personal information to open accounts or buy things in your name
questions.explain: Identity thieves use stolen details like Social Security numbers to commit fraud. Guarding that data and checking statements helps catch it early.

questions.q: Which password is the strongest?
options: Your pets name and birth year
A long passphrase of random words plus numbers and symbols
The same short password used everywhere
questions.explain: Length and uniqueness make passwords hard to crack. Using a different password for each account limits damage if one leaks.

questions.q: What does two-factor authentication add to an account?
options: A second password you tell friends
A second step, like a code sent to your phone, beyond your password
A backup copy of your password online
questions.explain: Two-factor authentication means a stolen password alone is not enough to break in. Turn it on for email, banking, and social accounts.

questions.q: A stranger online offers to send you a 1,000 dollar check if you send back 200 dollars in gift cards. What is this?
options: A safe way to earn quick money
A scam; the check will bounce and the gift cards will be gone
questions.explain: Fake check scams leave you owing the bank after the check bounces. Gift card payments are untraceable, which is why scammers demand them.

questions.q: What is a smart long-term financial goal for a teen?
options: Saving a set amount each month toward a first car or college costs
Having no plan and spending whatever is left
Keeping all money under a mattress forever
questions.explain: A written goal with a monthly amount turns saving into a habit. Specific goals are easier to reach than vague wishes.

questions.q: You want to save 1,200 dollars for a laptop in 12 months. How much should you set aside each month?
questions.explain: Divide 1,200 by 12 to get 100 dollars per month. Breaking a big goal into monthly steps makes it manageable.

questions.q: What is retirement saving, in simple terms?
options: A fee you pay when you quit a job
A loan you take at age 65
Putting money aside during your working years to live on when you stop working
questions.explain: Retirement accounts grow over decades, which is why starting young is powerful. Compound growth does much of the heavy lifting.

questions.q: Marta gets a call from someone claiming to be tech support who asks her to install software so they can fix her computer. What should she do?
options: Install it quickly so the problem does not spread
Give them her bank details to pay for the fix
Let them stay connected while she shops online
Hang up and contact the real company herself if she is worried
questions.explain: Real tech companies do not cold-call and demand remote access or payment. Hanging up and calling the official number keeps you in control.

title: Measuring Motion
subject: Physics Basics
description: Distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and reading simple motion from numbers and graphs.

questions.q: A runner covers 400 meters in 50 seconds. What is the average speed?
questions.explain: Speed equals distance divided by time: 400 divided by 50 equals 8 meters per second.

questions.q: A student walks 30 meters east, then 10 meters west. What is the displacement?
questions.explain: Displacement is final minus starting position: 30 east minus 10 west equals 20 meters east. Distance walked was 40 meters.

questions.q: Velocity differs from speed because velocity also includes:
questions.explain: Velocity is speed with direction, such as 10 meters per second north.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is:
questions.explain: If distance does not change as time passes, the object is at rest.

questions.q: A bus travels at a constant 15 meters per second for 20 seconds. How far does it go?
questions.explain: Distance equals speed times time: 15 times 20 equals 300 meters.

questions.q: Which is a vector quantity?
options: Velocity - it has magnitude and direction
questions.explain: Vectors have magnitude and direction. Velocity is a vector; speed, distance, and time are scalars.

questions.q: A cyclist's speed changes from rest in a straight line. Her position graph curves upward more steeply over time. This shows she is:
questions.explain: A distance-time graph that gets steeper shows speed is increasing.

questions.q: Instantaneous speed is:
options: The total distance divided by total time for a whole trip
The speed at one exact moment
The same as average speed on every trip
questions.explain: Instantaneous speed is what a speedometer shows at a single moment.

questions.q: A car goes 120 km in 2 hours, then 60 km in 1 hour. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
questions.explain: Total distance 180 km divided by total time 3 hours equals 60 km per hour.

questions.q: An object moves in a full circle and returns to its start. Its total displacement is:
questions.explain: Displacement depends only on start and end points. Returning to the start makes displacement zero, even though distance is not zero.

questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 100 / 2 = 50 mph.
questions.q: A car travels 100 miles in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

questions.explain: Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the center of the Earth.
questions.q: What force pulls objects toward the Earth?

questions.explain: Friction acts between surfaces that touch and always works against sliding motion.
options: A force that opposes motion between touching surfaces
A force that speeds objects up

questions.explain: This is also called the law of inertia: no net force means no change in motion.
options: Every action has an opposite reaction
Objects in motion stay in motion unless a force acts on them
questions.q: Newton's first law says:

questions.explain: F = m x a: force equals mass times acceleration.
questions.q: Newton's second law is written as:
You push a 2 kg box with a force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?

questions.explain: When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force.
options: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Objects at rest stay at rest

questions.explain: Speed = 60 / 10 = 6 m/s.
questions.q: A skateboarder rolls 60 meters in 10 seconds. What is the average speed?

questions.explain: Inertia is why you lurch forward when a car suddenly brakes.
options: An object's resistance to changes in its motion
questions.q: What is inertia?

questions.explain: Greater mass needs greater force for the same acceleration (F = m x a), and a car has far more mass than a bike.

subject: Physics Basics
title: Motion & Forces
Acceleration & Speed Changes
subject: Physics Basics
description: Acceleration as change in velocity, multi-step problems, and interpreting velocity-time graphs.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 meters per second to 30 meters per second in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration equals change in velocity divided by time: (30 minus 10) divided by 5 equals 4 meters per second squared.

questions.q: A bike slows from 12 meters per second to rest in 4 seconds. Its acceleration is:
options: 3 meters per second squared with speed increasing
questions.explain: Change is 0 minus 12 equals -12. Divided by 4 equals -3 meters per second squared; the negative sign shows slowing in the chosen direction.

questions.q: Starting from rest, an object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 6 seconds. Its final velocity is:
questions.explain: Final velocity equals acceleration times time from rest: 2 times 6 equals 12 meters per second.

questions.q: Using v squared style reasoning without symbols: a car at 20 meters per second brakes at 4 meters per second squared. How long until it stops?
questions.explain: Time equals change in velocity divided by deceleration: 20 divided by 4 equals 5 seconds.

questions.q: On a velocity-time graph, the slope of the line tells you the:
questions.explain: Slope of velocity versus time is change in velocity per time, which is acceleration.

questions.q: The area under a velocity-time graph tells you the:
questions.explain: Area under velocity-time (velocity times time) gives displacement.

questions.q: A sprinter reaches 9 meters per second in 3 seconds from rest, then holds that speed for 7 seconds. Total distance is closest to:
options: 76.5 meters - 13.5 during acceleration plus 63 at constant speed
questions.explain: During acceleration average speed is 4.5, times 3 equals 13.5 meters. Then 9 times 7 equals 63 meters. Total equals 76.5 meters.

questions.q: An object in free fall near Earth (ignoring air resistance) accelerates at about:
questions.explain: Gravity accelerates falling objects at about 9.8 meters per second squared near Earth's surface.

questions.q: A dropped ball (from rest, no air resistance) falls for 3 seconds. Its speed is about:
questions.explain: Speed equals g times t: 9.8 times 3 equals 29.4 meters per second.

questions.q: A train moving at 25 meters per second accelerates at 1.5 meters per second squared for 10 seconds. Its final speed is:
questions.explain: Final velocity equals initial plus a times t: 25 plus 1.5 times 10 equals 25 plus 15 equals 40 meters per second.

title: Newton's Laws in Action
subject: Physics Basics
description: Apply inertia, F equals m times a, and action-reaction to everyday scenarios and calculations.

questions.q: A 5 kg object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared. The net force is:
questions.explain: Net force equals mass times acceleration: 5 times 3 equals 15 newtons.

questions.q: A net force of 100 newtons acts on a 20 kg cart. Its acceleration is:
questions.explain: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 100 divided by 20 equals 5 meters per second squared.

questions.q: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes hard. This is best explained by:
options: Inertia - the body tends to keep moving (Newton's first law)
questions.explain: Inertia keeps the passenger moving forward while the bus slows - Newton's first law.

questions.q: When a rocket pushes exhaust gases down, the gases push the rocket up. This is:
options: Newton's third law - action and reaction
questions.explain: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction - Newton's third law.

questions.q: Two skaters push off each other. Skater A is 40 kg, skater B is 80 kg. Who accelerates more (same push force)?
options: Skater A - half the mass, so twice the acceleration
questions.explain: With the same force, acceleration equals force divided by mass, so the lighter skater accelerates twice as much.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The force pair for the book's weight (Earth pulls book down) by Newton's third law is:
options: The table pushes the book up (that is the normal force, a different interaction)
questions.explain: Third-law pairs act between the same two objects: Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls Earth. The table's normal force is a separate pair.

questions.q: What net force is needed to accelerate a 1200 kg car at 2.5 meters per second squared?
questions.explain: Force equals 1200 times 2.5 equals 3000 newtons.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball is thrown and air resistance is ignored after release (only gravity acts, downward). Its acceleration while in flight is:
options: About 9.8 meters per second squared downward the whole flight
Zero at the top only in the sense velocity is zero - acceleration is still downward (this full statement is the correct choice)
Upward on the way up, zero at top, downward on way down
Equal to its throwing force forever
questions.explain: Gravity acts the whole flight, so acceleration stays about 9.8 meters per second squared downward, even at the top where vertical velocity is momentarily zero.

questions.q: If the net force on an object is zero, the object:
options: Keeps its current velocity - at rest or moving steadily (Newton's first law)
questions.explain: Zero net force means no acceleration: velocity stays constant, which includes staying at rest.

questions.q: A 10 N force and a 6 N force act in opposite directions on a 2 kg object. Its acceleration is:
options: 2 meters per second squared in the direction of the 10 N force
questions.explain: Net force is 10 minus 6 equals 4 newtons. Acceleration equals 4 divided by 2 equals 2 meters per second squared.

title: Gravity, Mass & Weight

description: Distinguish mass from weight, use weight equals m times g, and explain orbits and falling.

questions.q: Mass and weight differ because:
options: Mass changes on the Moon but weight does not
Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location; weight is a force that depends on gravity
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Mass (in kilograms) is constant. Weight is mass times local gravity, measured in newtons, so it changes on the Moon.

questions.q: A student has a mass of 60 kg. On Earth (g about 10 meters per second squared for estimation), weight is about:
questions.explain: Weight equals m times g: 60 times 10 equals 600 newtons. Using 9.8 gives 588 newtons.

questions.q: On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's. A 60 kg student's Moon weight (using Earth weight 588 N) is about:
questions.explain: 588 divided by 6 equals 98 newtons. Mass stays 60 kg; only weight changes.

questions.q: Why do a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon (Apollo demonstration) but not on Earth?
options: There is almost no air on the Moon, so no air resistance slows the feather
Gravity is stronger for feathers on the Moon
The hammer becomes lighter than the feather
Feathers do not fall on Earth
questions.explain: Without air resistance, all objects accelerate at the same rate regardless of mass.

questions.q: An astronaut in orbit floats because:
options: There is no gravity in orbit
The astronaut and station are both in continuous free fall around Earth
Gravity is exactly zero at that height
questions.explain: Orbit is free fall: gravity still acts (about 90 percent of surface strength low in orbit) but both fall together around Earth.

questions.q: Which object has more inertia?
options: They are equal if speeds are equal
A loaded truck - more mass means more inertia
questions.explain: Inertia is resistance to changes in motion and increases with mass.

questions.q: A 3 kg object is dropped and a 3 kg object is thrown horizontally at the same instant (same height, no air resistance). Which hits the ground first?
options: Neither - the thrown one never falls
They hit at the same time
questions.explain: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both fall the same vertical distance in the same time.

questions.q: Gravitational force between two objects increases when:
options: Their masses increase or they move closer together
questions.explain: Gravity grows with mass and weakens quickly with distance (inverse-square).

questions.q: Weight on Earth of a 2 kg bag of sugar (g = 9.8) is:
questions.explain: Weight equals 2 times 9.8 equals 19.6 newtons. Kilograms measure mass, not weight.

questions.q: If Earth suddenly had twice its mass (same size), your weight would:
questions.explain: Weight is proportional to Earth's mass, so doubling Earth's mass roughly doubles surface gravity and your weight.

Work, Power & Machines
subject: Physics Basics
description: Work as force times distance, power, kinetic and potential energy calculations, and simple machines.

questions.q: You push a box with 50 newtons over 4 meters in the direction of motion. Work done is:
questions.explain: Work equals force times distance: 50 times 4 equals 200 joules.

questions.q: A machine does 600 joules of work in 10 seconds. Its power is:
questions.explain: Power equals work divided by time: 600 divided by 10 equals 60 watts.

questions.q: Kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 meters per second is:
questions.explain: Kinetic energy equals one-half m v squared: 0.5 times 2 times 9 equals 9 joules.

questions.q: Gravitational potential energy of a 5 kg book 2 meters above the floor (g = 10) is:
questions.explain: Potential energy equals m g h: 5 times 10 times 2 equals 100 joules.

questions.q: A lever lets you lift a heavy load with less force because:
options: It trades force for distance - you move the lever farther
It increases both force and distance for free
questions.explain: Simple machines trade force and distance; total work (ignoring friction) is not reduced.

questions.q: Carrying a heavy bag horizontally at constant height while walking at constant speed: work done BY gravity is:
options: Equal to weight times distance walked
Zero - gravity is perpendicular to the motion
questions.explain: Work requires force along the displacement. Gravity acts down, motion is horizontal, so gravity does no work in this ideal case.

questions.q: Two students climb the same stairs. Ana takes 10 seconds, Ben takes 20 seconds. Who developed more power (same weight and height)?
options: Ana - same work in less time means more power
questions.explain: Power equals work divided by time. Half the time means twice the power for the same work.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car at 20 meters per second has kinetic energy:
questions.explain: KE equals 0.5 times 1000 times 400 (20 squared) equals 200,000 joules.

questions.q: If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy:
options: Quadruples - it depends on speed squared
questions.explain: KE depends on v squared, so doubling speed multiplies KE by 4. That is why stopping distance grows so fast.

questions.q: Efficiency of a machine that takes in 500 joules and outputs 400 joules of useful work is:
questions.explain: Efficiency equals useful output divided by input times 100: 400 divided by 500 equals 0.8, or 80 percent. The rest is lost mainly as heat from friction.

Waves & Frequency
subject: Physics Basics
description: Wave speed, frequency, wavelength, amplitude, and how light and sound waves differ.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 5 hertz and wavelength 2 meters. Its speed is:
questions.explain: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 5 times 2 equals 10 meters per second.

questions.q: Frequency is measured in hertz, which means:
questions.explain: One hertz equals one cycle per second.

questions.q: A sound wave has speed 340 meters per second and frequency 170 hertz. Its wavelength is:
questions.explain: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency: 340 divided by 170 equals 2 meters.

questions.q: Amplitude of a wave is most related to:
options: How much energy it carries - loudness for sound, brightness for light
questions.explain: Larger amplitude means more energy: louder sounds and brighter light.

questions.q: Which correctly orders parts of the electromagnetic spectrum from longest wavelength to shortest?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
questions.explain: Wavelength decreases (and frequency and energy increase) from radio through gamma rays.

questions.q: A wave's period is 0.25 seconds. Its frequency is:
questions.explain: Frequency equals 1 divided by period: 1 divided by 0.25 equals 4 hertz.

questions.q: When a wave passes from air into water and slows, its wavelength:
questions.explain: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same, so slower speed means shorter wavelength (refraction).

questions.q: Ultrasound used in medical imaging is:
options: Sound with frequency too high for humans to hear (above about 20,000 hertz)
questions.explain: Ultrasound means frequencies above human hearing, above about 20,000 hertz. Below 20 hertz is infrasound.

questions.q: Light travels in vacuum at about:
options: 300,000,000 meters per second (3 times 10 to the 8th)
questions.explain: The speed of light in vacuum, c, is about 3 times 10 to the 8th meters per second. 340 is the speed of sound in air.

questions.q: Two waves have the same speed. Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B. Wave A's wavelength is:
questions.explain: At fixed speed, wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, so doubling frequency halves wavelength.

title: Electricity & Circuits
subject: Physics Basics
description: Voltage, current, resistance with Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, and electrical power - with multi-step problems.

questions.q: Ohm's law states voltage equals:
options: Current times resistance (V = I times R)
questions.explain: Ohm's law: V equals I times R. Rearrange to find current or resistance as needed.

questions.q: A 12 volt battery is connected to a 4 ohm resistor. The current is:
questions.explain: Current equals voltage divided by resistance: 12 divided by 4 equals 3 amperes.

questions.q: A circuit has current 2 amperes and resistance 10 ohms. The voltage needed is:
questions.explain: Voltage equals current times resistance: 2 times 10 equals 20 volts.

questions.q: Two 6 ohm resistors in series have a total resistance of:
questions.explain: Series resistances add: 6 plus 6 equals 12 ohms.

questions.q: Two 6 ohm resistors in parallel have a total resistance of:
questions.explain: For two equal resistors in parallel, total is half of one: 6 divided by 2 equals 3 ohms. In general 1 over R total equals sum of 1 over each.

questions.q: A 9 volt battery drives a series circuit with a 2 ohm and a 7 ohm resistor. Current everywhere in the series loop is:
questions.explain: Total resistance is 2 plus 7 equals 9 ohms. Current equals 9 divided by 9 equals 1 ampere, the same at every point in series.

questions.q: Electrical power for a device with voltage 120 volts and current 5 amperes is:
questions.explain: Power equals voltage times current: 120 times 5 equals 600 watts.

questions.q: A 100 watt bulb runs for 3 hours. Energy used (in kilowatt-hours) is:
questions.explain: Energy equals power in kilowatts times hours: 0.1 kW times 3 equals 0.3 kilowatt-hours.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, if one branch bulb burns out, the other branches:
options: Stay lit - each branch has its own path
questions.explain: Parallel branches are independent paths, so one open branch does not break the others. Voltage across each branch stays the same (ideal).

questions.q: Multi-step: A 24 volt source connects to a parallel pair: branch 1 is 8 ohms, branch 2 is 24 ohms. Total current from the source is:
options: 4 amperes - 3 A through 8 ohms plus 1 A through 24 ohms
questions.explain: Branch currents: 24 divided by 8 equals 3 A, and 24 divided by 24 equals 1 A. Parallel currents add: 3 plus 1 equals 4 amperes.

title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Ask questions, form hypotheses, and plan fair tests.

questions.q: What is usually the first step of a scientific investigation?
options: Ask a question based on an observation
Publish the results in a journal
questions.explain: Investigations start with noticing something and asking a question about it.

questions.q: A hypothesis is best described as...
options: the final conclusion of an experiment
a testable prediction that can be supported or not by data
a random guess with no evidence
a proven fact that never changes
questions.explain: A hypothesis is an if-then prediction that an experiment can test.

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment several times?
options: Because the first result is always wrong
To make the experiment take longer
To check that the results are consistent and reliable
questions.explain: Repeated trials show whether results are consistent and trustworthy.

questions.q: After collecting data in an experiment, what should a scientist do next?
options: Change the hypothesis to match any result
Throw away data that looks unusual
Analyze the data and look for patterns
questions.explain: Data must be organized and analyzed before conclusions are drawn.

questions.q: A conclusion of an experiment should mainly state...
options: whether the data supported the hypothesis
how much fun the experiment was
questions.explain: The conclusion explains whether the evidence supported the hypothesis.

questions.q: Which of these is an observation?
options: The puddle came from a water balloon fight
Someone must have spilled the puddle on purpose
The puddle will be gone by lunch
The puddle on the sidewalk is 2 meters wide
questions.explain: An observation reports what is directly seen or measured: the puddle is 2 meters wide.

questions.q: You walk outside in the morning and see wet grass. Which statement is an inference?
options: Droplets are visible on the leaves
The sky is cloudy right now
questions.explain: Saying it rained is an inference - a conclusion drawn from the observation of wet grass.

questions.q: Why is peer review important in science?
options: Other scientists check the work for errors before it is widely accepted
It lets scientists copy each other's answers
It replaces the need for evidence
questions.explain: Peer review catches mistakes and weak evidence before results are accepted.

questions.q: Why should an experiment change only one variable at a time?
options: So the scientist can tell which change caused the results
To make the data table smaller
Because lab equipment can only measure one thing
To finish the experiment more quickly
questions.explain: Changing one variable at a time lets you link the cause to the effect.

questions.q: Results that do NOT support a hypothesis should lead a scientist to...
options: revise the hypothesis and test again
questions.explain: Unsupported results are still useful; they guide a better hypothesis and a new test.

questions.q: Which statement about scientific theories is correct?
options: Theories cannot be changed by new evidence
A theory becomes a law when it gets old enough
Theories are explanations supported by large amounts of evidence
Theories are guesses that have not been tested
questions.explain: A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation, not a guess.

questions.q: A student claims plants grow better with more water after testing only one plant one time. What is the biggest problem with this claim?
options: The sample is too small and the test was not repeated
One plant is too expensive to test
Plants do not need water to grow
questions.explain: Reliable claims need many trials and repeated results, not a single test.

questions.q: Which term means: a testable prediction about what will happen in an experiment?
questions.explain: The term 'hypothesis' means a testable prediction about what will happen in an experiment.

questions.q: Which term means: information gathered using the senses or scientific tools?
questions.explain: The term 'observation' means information gathered using the senses or scientific tools.

questions.q: What does the term 'inference' mean?
options: facts and information collected during an investigation
data that describe qualities, such as color, texture, or smell
a conclusion drawn from observations and prior knowledge
how close a set of measurements are to one another
questions.explain: 'Inference' means a conclusion drawn from observations and prior knowledge.

questions.q: Which term means: facts and information collected during an investigation?
questions.explain: The term 'data' means facts and information collected during an investigation.

questions.q: Sofia wants to find out whether the amount of sunlight affects how tall tomato plants grow. She gives three plants different amounts of sunlight each day and measures their heights after four weeks. What is the independent variable?
questions.explain: The independent variable is the factor changed on purpose: the amount of sunlight.

questions.q: Marcus tests whether the brand of paper towel affects how much water it can absorb. He dips each brand in water for ten seconds and measures the water absorbed. What is the dependent variable?
options: size of the paper towel pieces
questions.explain: The dependent variable is what is measured: the amount of water absorbed.

questions.q: A class investigates whether temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves in water. They stir sugar into water at different temperatures and time how long it takes to disappear. Which of these is a constant in this experiment?
options: time for the sugar to dissolve
questions.explain: A constant is kept the same; here the amount of water stays the same.

questions.q: Lena checks whether listening to music changes how fast students finish a puzzle. Some students work in silence and others listen to music while timing their puzzle solving. What is the independent variable?
options: time needed to finish the puzzle
questions.explain: The independent variable is the factor changed on purpose: the whether music is playing.

rounds.title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Ask questions, form hypotheses, and plan fair tests.

title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Identify independent and dependent variables, constants, and control groups.

questions.q: Jayden tests whether the type of music affects how fast he finishes homework. What is the independent variable?
options: how fast the homework is finished
questions.explain: The independent variable is what Jayden changes on purpose: the type of music.

questions.q: In Jayden's music-and-homework test, what is the dependent variable?
options: how fast the homework is finished
questions.explain: The dependent variable is the outcome that gets measured: finishing speed.

questions.q: A scientist tests whether fertilizer makes roses bloom more. The group of roses that gets NO fertilizer is the...
questions.explain: The control group gets no treatment and provides a comparison.

questions.q: Why does an experiment need a control group?
options: It gives a baseline to compare the experimental group against
It uses up the extra plants
It guarantees the hypothesis is correct
It makes the experiment look more official
questions.explain: Comparing with a control group shows whether the treatment actually made a difference.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY constants for an experiment testing if heat affects how fast ice melts? All cups get the same size ice cube, the same cup, and the same room lighting.
options: temperature, ice cube size, melting time
same ice cube size, same cup, same room lighting
questions.explain: Constants are the factors kept identical: cube size, cup, and lighting.

questions.q: An experiment has a mistake: the plants with fertilizer also got more sunlight than the plants without fertilizer. What is this problem called?
questions.explain: When another factor changes along with the treatment, it confounds the results.

questions.q: Which experimental design would give the MOST reliable results?
options: Test 2 plants per group and stop early when results look good
Test 30 plants per group and repeat the whole experiment twice
Test 3 plants per group one time
Test 1 plant per group one time
questions.explain: Larger samples and repeated trials produce more reliable results.

questions.q: A hypothesis for an experiment on bounce height might be: 'If a ball is dropped from a greater height, then it will bounce higher.' The dependent variable is...
questions.explain: Bounce height is the measured result, so it is the dependent variable.

questions.q: In the bounce-height hypothesis, the independent variable is...
questions.explain: Drop height is what the scientist changes on purpose.

questions.q: A student measures plant growth every day for two weeks and records it in a table. The table is an example of...
questions.explain: Recorded measurements organized in a table are data.

questions.q: Which question can be answered by a scientific experiment?
options: Does adding salt make water boil at a higher temperature?
questions.explain: Only testable questions about measurable effects can be answered by experiment; the others are opinions.

questions.q: Two groups of mice are fed the same food and kept in identical cages. One group gets a vitamin supplement. After a month, the scientist compares their masses. What is the independent variable?
options: whether the mice get the vitamin supplement
questions.explain: The supplement is the one factor changed on purpose between the groups.

questions.q: Which term means: the factor that the scientist changes on purpose in an experiment?
questions.explain: The term 'independent variable' means the factor that the scientist changes on purpose in an experiment.

questions.q: Which term means: the factor that is measured or observed as the result of an experiment?
questions.explain: The term 'dependent variable' means the factor that is measured or observed as the result of an experiment.

questions.q: What does the term 'constant' mean?
options: how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
a well-tested explanation that ties together a broad range of observations
a factor that is kept the same throughout an experiment
the amount of space that an object or substance takes up
questions.explain: 'Constant' means a factor that is kept the same throughout an experiment.

questions.q: Which term means: the group in an experiment that does not receive the independent variable and is used for comparison?
questions.explain: The term 'control group' means the group in an experiment that does not receive the independent variable and is used for comparison.

questions.q: Lena checks whether listening to music changes how fast students finish a puzzle. Some students work in silence and others listen to music while timing their puzzle solving. What is the dependent variable?
options: time needed to finish the puzzle
questions.explain: The dependent variable is what is measured: the time needed to finish the puzzle.

questions.q: A gardener tests whether fertilizer helps bean plants produce more beans. Two groups of plants get the same water and sunlight, but only one group gets fertilizer. Which of these is a constant in this experiment?
questions.explain: A constant is kept the same; here the amount of water stays the same.

questions.q: Noah studies whether the height of a ramp changes how far a toy car rolls. He releases the car from ramps of different heights and measures the distance it travels. What is the independent variable?
questions.explain: The independent variable is the factor changed on purpose: the height of the ramp.

questions.q: Sofia wants to find out whether the amount of sunlight affects how tall tomato plants grow. She gives three plants different amounts of sunlight each day and measures their heights after four weeks. What is the dependent variable?
questions.explain: The dependent variable is what is measured: the height of the tomato plants.

rounds.title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Identify independent and dependent variables, constants, and control groups.

title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Measure with SI units and the right tools, and convert between metric units.

questions.q: Which tool is used to measure the mass of a rock sample?
questions.explain: A triple-beam balance measures mass.

questions.q: Which tool is best for measuring the volume of a liquid?
questions.explain: A graduated cylinder is designed to measure liquid volume in milliliters.

questions.q: What is the SI unit for measuring length?
questions.explain: The meter is the SI base unit of length.

questions.q: To read the volume of a liquid correctly, you should...
options: read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level
tilt the cylinder until it looks full
read the top of the curve from above
estimate between the marks without looking closely
questions.explain: Volumes are read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus.

questions.q: How can you find the volume of an irregularly shaped stone?
options: Drop it in a graduated cylinder and measure how much the water level rises
Weigh it on a balance and divide by two
Place it next to a cube and guess
Measure its length with a ruler and multiply by its color
questions.explain: Water displacement: the rise in water level equals the stone's volume.

questions.q: Why do scientists around the world use the metric (SI) system?
options: It is only used in science classes
It is the oldest system of measurement
It makes every measurement a whole number
It gives everyone the same standard units so results can be compared
questions.explain: Shared standard units let scientists everywhere compare and repeat results.

questions.q: A thermometer in a science lab usually measures temperature in...
questions.explain: School lab thermometers are marked in degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which measurement is quantitative data?
options: The beaker holds 250 milliliters of water
questions.explain: Quantitative data uses numbers: 250 milliliters.

questions.q: Which measurement is qualitative data?
options: The solution has a mass of 12 grams
questions.explain: Qualitative data describes qualities, like color, without numbers.

questions.q: A paperclip is placed on a ruler. It starts at the 2 cm mark and ends at the 5 cm mark. How long is the paperclip?
questions.explain: Length = 5 cm - 2 cm = 3 cm.

questions.q: Which set of measurements shows the GREATEST precision? The true value is about 10 grams.
questions.explain: Precision means the measurements are close to each other: 10.1, 10.2, 10.1.

questions.q: A student measures the same book three times: 24 cm, 24 cm, 24 cm. The actual length is 30 cm. These measurements are...
questions.explain: The values agree with each other (precise) but are far from the true value (not accurate).

questions.q: What does the term 'mass' mean?
options: a tall, narrow container used to measure the volume of a liquid
an enclosed workspace that pulls harmful fumes away from the user
the amount of matter in an object, usually measured in grams
an instrument used to measure the mass of an object
questions.explain: 'Mass' means the amount of matter in an object, usually measured in grams.

questions.q: Which term means: the amount of space that an object or substance takes up?
questions.explain: The term 'volume' means the amount of space that an object or substance takes up.

questions.q: Which term means: a tall, narrow container used to measure the volume of a liquid?
questions.explain: The term 'graduated cylinder' means a tall, narrow container used to measure the volume of a liquid.

questions.q: What does the term 'meniscus' mean?
options: the amount of matter in an object, usually measured in grams
a heavy blanket used to smother flames on a person or a small fire
the curved surface of a liquid in a container, read at its lowest point
a factor that is kept the same throughout an experiment
questions.explain: 'Meniscus' means the curved surface of a liquid in a container, read at its lowest point.

questions.q: Convert: 4 liters is equal to how many milliliters?
questions.explain: Multiply or divide by 1000 to convert from liters to milliliters.

questions.q: Convert: 3 minutes is equal to how many seconds?
questions.explain: Multiply or divide by 60 to convert from minutes to seconds.

questions.q: Convert: 2 minutes is equal to how many seconds?
questions.explain: Multiply or divide by 60 to convert from minutes to seconds.

questions.q: A student timed a reaction four times. The measurements are 19, 5, 13, 27 seconds. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

rounds.title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Measure with SI units and the right tools, and convert between metric units.

title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: lab safety rules and reading data tables and graphs.

questions.q: When heating a chemical in a test tube, you should always...
options: point the open end away from yourself and others
hold your thumb over the opening
heat it with the cap sealed tightly on
point it toward your partner to show them
questions.explain: Heated liquids can splash out; the opening must point away from people.

questions.q: To smell a chemical safely in the lab, you should...
options: shake the container near your face
put your nose directly over the container
waft the vapors toward your nose with your hand
ask a partner to smell it first
questions.explain: Wafting brings a small amount of vapor to your nose without a direct inhalation.

questions.q: A student breaks a glass beaker. What is the safest action?
options: Pick up the pieces with bare hands
Leave it and let the next class find it
Kick the pieces under the table
Tell the teacher, then use a broom and dustpan to put the glass in the broken-glass container
questions.explain: Broken glass is swept up (never touched by hand) and placed in the glass disposal container.

questions.q: If a chemical splashes into your eyes, you should...
options: rinse your eyes at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes and tell the teacher
rub your eyes until they feel better
blink quickly for ten seconds and continue
wait until the end of class to rinse
questions.explain: Eyes exposed to chemicals need long, immediate rinsing at the eyewash station.

questions.q: Why should long hair and loose sleeves be tied back during labs?
options: They make it harder to write in a notebook
They change the results of experiments
They could catch fire or knock over equipment
questions.explain: Loose hair and clothing are fire and spill hazards in the lab.

questions.q: What should you do before starting any lab activity?
options: Read all the directions and listen to the teacher's instructions
Mix the chemicals to see what happens
questions.explain: Reading directions first prevents accidents and mistakes.

questions.q: A classmate's clothing catches fire. The fastest safe response is...
options: use the fire blanket to smother the flames and alert the teacher
fan the flames with a notebook
pour a bucket of chemicals on it
questions.explain: A fire blanket smothers flames on clothing; running makes fire worse.

questions.q: Why is eating and drinking forbidden in the science lab?
options: It is against school dress code
Food and drinks can become contaminated with chemicals
questions.explain: Chemicals can get onto food and be swallowed, so eating in the lab is unsafe.

questions.q: When should safety goggles be worn?
options: Only when the teacher is watching
Whenever chemicals, heat, or glassware are being used
questions.explain: Goggles protect eyes during any work with chemicals, heat, or glass.

questions.q: Which graph is best for showing how plant height changed over 14 days?
options: a bar graph of different plant types
a picture graph of favorite plants
questions.explain: Line graphs show how a measurement changes over time.

questions.q: Which graph is best for comparing the masses of four different rocks?
questions.explain: Bar graphs compare amounts across separate categories.

questions.q: A class measured the temperature every hour. At 9 AM it was 18 degrees Celsius and at noon it was 27 degrees Celsius. What happened to the temperature?
questions.explain: 27 - 18 = 9, so the temperature rose by 9 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which term means: safety equipment used to rinse chemicals out of the eyes?
questions.explain: The term 'eyewash station' means safety equipment used to rinse chemicals out of the eyes.

questions.q: Which term means: a heavy blanket used to smother flames on a person or a small fire?
questions.explain: The term 'fire blanket' means a heavy blanket used to smother flames on a person or a small fire.

questions.q: What does the term 'precision' mean?
options: the factor that the scientist changes on purpose in an experiment
how close a set of measurements are to one another
a tall, narrow container used to measure the volume of a liquid
the group in an experiment that does not receive the independent variable and is used for comparison
questions.explain: 'Precision' means how close a set of measurements are to one another.

questions.q: What does the term 'accuracy' mean?
options: information gathered using the senses or scientific tools
data that describe qualities, such as color, texture, or smell
the factor that is measured or observed as the result of an experiment
how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
questions.explain: 'Accuracy' means how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value.

questions.q: Four groups measured the length of a leaf. The measurements are 25, 28, 13, 30 centimeters. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

questions.q: A student recorded the temperature of a classroom four times. The measurements are 11, 29, 29, 7 degrees Celsius. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

questions.q: Convert: 200 centimeters is equal to how many meters?
questions.explain: Multiply or divide by the metric factor to convert from centimeters to meters.

questions.q: Convert: 2 meters is equal to how many centimeters?
questions.explain: Multiply or divide by 100 to convert from meters to centimeters.

rounds.title: Science Skills & Lab Safety - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: lab safety rules and reading data tables and graphs.

title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Explore cell structure and the jobs of the major organelles.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of life?
questions.explain: All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life.

questions.q: Which organelle releases energy from glucose and is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.explain: Mitochondria release energy from glucose during cellular respiration.

questions.q: Which structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
questions.explain: The cell membrane is selectively permeable and controls movement in and out.

questions.q: The nucleus of a cell is important because it...
options: contains DNA and directs the cell's activities
questions.explain: The nucleus holds the genetic instructions (DNA) that direct the cell.

questions.q: Photosynthesis takes place inside which organelle?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts capture sunlight for photosynthesis in plant cells.

questions.q: Which structure gives a plant cell its rigid shape and extra protection?
questions.explain: The cell wall is a rigid outer layer found in plant cells.

questions.q: The jelly-like fluid that fills a cell and holds the organelles is called...
questions.explain: Cytoplasm is the gel-like fluid inside the cell.

questions.q: Proteins are built in which small cell structure?
questions.explain: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell is a very large sac that stores water and keeps the cell firm?
questions.explain: The large central vacuole stores water and helps support the plant cell.

questions.q: How does a plant cell differ from an animal cell?
options: A plant cell has a cell wall and chloroplasts; an animal cell does not
A plant cell has a nucleus; an animal cell does not
An animal cell has chloroplasts; a plant cell does not
A plant cell is not made of cells
questions.explain: Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not animal cells.

questions.q: What makes a eukaryotic cell different from a prokaryotic cell?
options: A eukaryotic cell has no DNA
A eukaryotic cell has a membrane-bound nucleus
A prokaryotic cell is always larger
questions.explain: Eukaryotes have a true nucleus; prokaryotes, like bacteria, do not.

questions.q: Why do scientists need microscopes to study most cells?
options: Most cells are too small to be seen with the unaided eye
Cells move too quickly to look at
questions.explain: Most cells are microscopic, so magnification is needed to see them.

questions.q: Which term means: the thin barrier around a cell that controls what enters and leaves?
questions.explain: The term 'cell membrane' means the thin barrier around a cell that controls what enters and leaves.

questions.q: Which term means: the organelle that contains DNA and directs the activities of the cell?
questions.explain: The term 'nucleus' means the organelle that contains DNA and directs the activities of the cell.

questions.q: Which term means: the organelle that releases energy from glucose during cellular respiration?
questions.explain: The term 'mitochondria' means the organelle that releases energy from glucose during cellular respiration.

questions.q: Which term means: the organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place?
questions.explain: The term 'chloroplast' means the organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.

questions.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece lens and a 10x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 10 x 10 = 100x.

questions.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece lens and a 40x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 10 x 40 = 400x.

questions.q: A microscope has a 15x eyepiece lens and a 100x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 15 x 100 = 1500x.

questions.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece lens and a 4x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 10 x 4 = 40x.

rounds.title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Explore cell structure and the jobs of the major organelles.

title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Photosynthesis, respiration, diffusion, and osmosis move energy and materials.

questions.q: Which equation correctly shows photosynthesis?
options: carbon dioxide + water + sunlight -> glucose + oxygen
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight to build glucose and release oxygen.

questions.q: Which equation correctly shows cellular respiration?
options: carbon dioxide + water + sunlight -> glucose + oxygen
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.explain: Respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen, releasing energy, carbon dioxide, and water.

questions.q: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related?
options: Photosynthesis releases the energy stored in glucose
The products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the reactants of respiration
They are the exact same process
questions.explain: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; respiration releases it, using the oxygen photosynthesis made.

questions.q: When you open a bottle of perfume, the scent slowly spreads through the room. This is an example of...
questions.explain: Particles spread from high concentration to low concentration by diffusion.

questions.q: A wilted houseplant is watered and becomes firm again. What process moved water into its cells?
questions.explain: Water moved across cell membranes by osmosis, refilling the vacuoles.

questions.q: A freshwater fish's cells are placed in very salty water in a lab dish. What will happen to the cells?
options: The cells will turn into salt crystals
Nothing, because cell walls block all water
Water will leave the cells by osmosis and the cells will shrink
Water will rush in until the cells burst, guaranteed
questions.explain: Water moves toward the saltier side, so water leaves the cells and they shrink.

questions.q: What is the main difference between passive transport and active transport?
options: Active transport moves particles from low to high numbers randomly
Passive transport happens only in animal cells
Active transport requires energy from the cell; passive transport does not
questions.explain: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy.

questions.q: Why do muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells?
options: Muscle cells are larger than all other cells
Skin cells do not use any energy
Muscle cells need much more energy to contract and move
questions.explain: More mitochondria release more energy, which hard-working muscle cells need.

questions.q: Which gas do plant cells take in from the air for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants absorb carbon dioxide through their leaves for photosynthesis.

questions.q: Where does almost all of the energy for life on Earth originally come from?
questions.explain: Sunlight powers photosynthesis, which feeds nearly all food webs.

questions.q: A cell keeps its internal conditions steady, even when the outside changes. This is called...
questions.explain: Homeostasis is maintaining stable internal conditions.

questions.q: Which of these does a plant cell need to carry out photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis requires light energy, carbon dioxide, and water.

questions.q: Which term means: the movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration?
questions.explain: The term 'diffusion' means the movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

questions.q: Which term means: the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane?
questions.explain: The term 'osmosis' means the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.q: What does the term 'photosynthesis' mean?
options: the process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and oxygen
the organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place
a storage sac in a cell that holds water, food, or waste
the thin barrier around a cell that controls what enters and leaves
questions.explain: 'Photosynthesis' means the process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: What does the term 'cellular respiration' mean?
options: the process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and oxygen
the process that breaks down glucose with oxygen to release energy for the cell
the organelle that contains DNA and directs the activities of the cell
the thin barrier around a cell that controls what enters and leaves
questions.explain: 'Cellular respiration' means the process that breaks down glucose with oxygen to release energy for the cell.

questions.q: A drop of dye spreads 6 centimeters through a gel in 3 minutes. At what average rate did it spread?
questions.explain: Rate = distance divided by time. Rate = 6 / 3 = 2.

questions.q: An aquatic plant under a lamp produces 6 oxygen bubbles in 2 minutes. How many bubbles per minute is that?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, so the bubble rate measures the rate of photosynthesis. Rate = 6 / 2 = 3.

questions.q: During an experiment, a plant in sunlight released 30 bubbles of oxygen in 5 minutes, while a plant in the dark released none. What do the bubbles show?
options: Respiration stopped completely in the light
Photosynthesis happened in the light but not in the dark
questions.explain: Oxygen bubbles are a product of photosynthesis, which needs light.

questions.q: A cell uses energy to move a substance from a region where it is scarce to a region where it is already plentiful. This is an example of...
questions.explain: Moving against the concentration gradient requires energy: active transport.

rounds.title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Photosynthesis, respiration, diffusion, and osmosis move energy and materials.

title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Mitosis, DNA, and the levels of organization from cell to organism.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of mitosis in a multicellular organism?
options: growth and repair of body tissues
questions.explain: Mitosis produces new body cells for growth and to repair damage.

questions.q: A cell divides by mitosis. The two new cells are...
options: genetically identical to the parent cell
each missing half of the parent's organs
questions.explain: Mitosis copies the DNA so daughter cells are genetically identical.

questions.q: Which list shows the levels of organization in the correct order, from smallest to largest?
options: tissue -> cell -> organ -> organism -> organ system
cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism
organism -> organ system -> organ -> tissue -> cell
cell -> organ -> tissue -> organism -> organ system
questions.explain: Organization builds from cells to tissues, organs, organ systems, and the whole organism.

questions.q: Your heart is an example of which level of organization?
questions.explain: The heart is an organ made of muscle, nerve, and connective tissues.

questions.q: A group of muscle cells working together to contract is an example of...
questions.explain: Similar cells working together form a tissue.

questions.q: What are chromosomes made of?
questions.explain: Chromosomes consist of DNA wrapped around proteins.

questions.q: Why must DNA be copied before a cell divides?
options: So the cell can become larger
So the parent cell can store extra food
So each new cell receives a complete set of instructions
So chromosomes can leave the cell
questions.explain: Copying DNA first ensures both daughter cells get the full instruction set.

questions.q: Cancer is a disease in which cells...
questions.explain: Cancer results from cells dividing without normal controls.

questions.q: How many daughter cells does one round of mitosis produce from a single parent cell?
questions.explain: Mitosis produces two daughter cells.

questions.q: A single-celled amoeba is a complete...
questions.explain: A unicellular living thing is a whole organism made of one cell.

questions.q: Stem cells are important in medicine because they can...
options: stop all cell division in the body
develop into many different types of cells
questions.explain: Stem cells can specialize into different cell types, which may repair tissues.

questions.q: Before mitosis begins, what must happen to the cell's chromosomes?
options: They combine into a single chromosome
They leave the nucleus and dissolve
They are copied so there are two complete sets
questions.explain: Chromosomes replicate during interphase so division can share them equally.

questions.q: Which term means: cell division that produces two identical daughter cells from one parent cell?
questions.explain: The term 'mitosis' means cell division that produces two identical daughter cells from one parent cell.

questions.q: Which term means: a group of similar cells that work together to perform one function?
questions.explain: The term 'tissue' means a group of similar cells that work together to perform one function.

questions.q: What does the term 'organ' mean?
options: the molecule that carries the genetic instructions of a cell
the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane
the rigid outer layer of a plant cell that gives support and protection
a structure made of different tissues working together, such as the heart or a leaf
questions.explain: 'Organ' means a structure made of different tissues working together, such as the heart or a leaf.

questions.q: Which term means: one complete living thing?
questions.explain: The term 'organism' means one complete living thing.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 4 bacteria, how many are there after 3 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 4 x 2^3 = 32.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 3 bacteria, how many are there after 2 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 3 x 2^2 = 12.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 5 bacteria, how many are there after 3 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 5 x 2^3 = 40.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 4 bacteria, how many are there after 5 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 4 x 2^5 = 128.

rounds.title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Mitosis, DNA, and the levels of organization from cell to organism.

title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: classification, bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

questions.q: Bacteria are classified as prokaryotes because they...
questions.explain: Bacterial cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus, so they are prokaryotes.

questions.q: Why is a virus NOT considered a living thing?
options: It is not made of cells and cannot reproduce on its own
It is too small to see
questions.explain: Viruses are not cells and must infect a host cell to reproduce, so they are nonliving.

questions.q: Which of these is a helpful role of bacteria?
options: Decomposing dead matter and recycling nutrients
questions.explain: Decomposer bacteria recycle nutrients back into ecosystems.

questions.q: Antibiotics are used to treat infections caused by...
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacteria; they do not work on viruses like the flu.

questions.q: Which kingdom includes organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis and have cell walls?
questions.explain: Plants photosynthesize and have rigid cell walls.

questions.q: Fungi such as mushrooms get their food by...
questions.explain: Most fungi are decomposers that absorb nutrients from dead material.

questions.q: A dichotomous key helps a scientist to...
options: identify an unknown organism by answering paired questions
measure the mass of an organism
keep organisms alive in a lab
questions.explain: A dichotomous key uses a series of either-or choices to identify organisms.

questions.q: Why do scientists give every species a unique two-part scientific name?
options: To make names longer and harder to spell
So scientists everywhere use the same name and avoid confusion
questions.explain: Binomial names are universal, while common names vary by place and language.

questions.q: Which practice best prevents the spread of many bacterial and viral diseases?
options: Washing hands with soap and water
questions.explain: Handwashing removes microbes and reduces disease transmission.

questions.q: Yogurt and some cheeses are made with the help of...
questions.explain: Certain bacteria ferment milk sugars, producing yogurt and cheese.

questions.q: Which organism is single-celled and has a nucleus?
questions.explain: An amoeba is a unicellular eukaryote - one cell with a nucleus.

questions.q: Mold growing on old bread is a member of which group?
questions.explain: Molds are fungi, decomposers that absorb nutrients from their food source.

questions.q: Which term means: single-celled organisms that do not have a nucleus?
questions.explain: The term 'bacteria' means single-celled organisms that do not have a nucleus.

questions.q: Which term means: a nonliving particle of genetic material in a protein coat that must infect a living cell to reproduce?
questions.explain: The term 'virus' means a nonliving particle of genetic material in a protein coat that must infect a living cell to reproduce.

questions.q: What does the term 'DNA' mean?
options: the process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and oxygen
a nonliving particle of genetic material in a protein coat that must infect a living cell to reproduce
the molecule that carries the genetic instructions of a cell
questions.explain: 'Dna' means the molecule that carries the genetic instructions of a cell.

questions.q: What does the term 'cell' mean?
options: the small cell structure where proteins are built
the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane
the organelle that releases energy from glucose during cellular respiration
the smallest unit of life and the basic building block of all living things
questions.explain: 'Cell' means the smallest unit of life and the basic building block of all living things.

questions.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece lens and a 100x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 10 x 100 = 1000x.

questions.q: A microscope has a 15x eyepiece lens and a 40x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece x objective = 15 x 40 = 600x.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 3 bacteria, how many are there after 3 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 3 x 2^3 = 24.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 5 bacteria, how many are there after 5 rounds of division?
questions.explain: Each round doubles the count: 5 x 2^5 = 160.

rounds.title: Cells & Living Things - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: classification, bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

title: Human Body Systems - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Bones, joints, and muscles support and move the body.

questions.q: What are the main jobs of the skeletal system?
options: Support the body, protect organs, store minerals, and make blood cells
Take in oxygen from the air
questions.explain: Bones support and protect the body, store minerals, and produce blood cells in the marrow.

questions.q: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton (approximately)?
questions.explain: An adult has about 206 bones; babies have more that fuse with age.

questions.q: Which type of joint allows the arm to rotate in a full circle at the shoulder?
questions.explain: The shoulder's ball-and-socket joint allows the widest range of motion.

questions.q: The knee and elbow work mainly as which type of joint?
questions.explain: Hinge joints bend in one direction, like a door hinge.

questions.q: Muscles move bones by...
options: contracting (shortening) and pulling on the bones
questions.explain: Muscles can only pull; they contract to pull bones at joints.

questions.q: Why do muscles often work in pairs, such as the biceps and triceps?
options: One muscle can rest forever while the other works
One muscle bends the joint while the other straightens it
questions.explain: Because muscles only pull, pairs work in opposite directions across a joint.

questions.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.explain: Tendons attach muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone.

questions.q: What connects one bone to another bone at a joint?
questions.explain: Ligaments hold bones together at joints.

questions.q: What is the role of cartilage at the ends of bones?
options: It cushions the joint and reduces friction
It makes the bone grow taller
questions.explain: Smooth cartilage covers bone ends so joints move without grinding.

questions.q: Which muscle type is found in the walls of the stomach and intestines and works without conscious control?
questions.explain: Smooth muscle moves food through the digestive tract involuntarily.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is found only in...
questions.explain: Cardiac muscle makes up the heart walls and pumps blood.

questions.q: Exercise makes bones stronger mainly because...
options: bones grow a new outer skin
stress on bones signals the body to build more bone tissue
questions.explain: Weight-bearing activity stimulates bone-building cells, increasing bone density.

questions.q: Which term means: the body system of bones that supports the body, protects organs, and makes blood cells?
questions.explain: The term 'skeletal system' means the body system of bones that supports the body, protects organs, and makes blood cells.

questions.q: Which term means: the body system of muscles that moves the body and its internal parts?
questions.explain: The term 'muscular system' means the body system of muscles that moves the body and its internal parts.

questions.q: Which term means: tough tissue that connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.explain: The term 'tendon' means tough tissue that connects a muscle to a bone.

questions.q: Which term means: tough tissue that connects one bone to another bone at a joint?
questions.explain: The term 'ligament' means tough tissue that connects one bone to another bone at a joint.

questions.q: A student counts 22 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 22 x 4 = 88 beats per minute.

questions.q: A student counts 14 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 14 x 4 = 56 beats per minute.

questions.q: A coach measured a runner's resting heart rate on four mornings. The measurements are 14, 6, 17, 11 beats per minute. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

questions.q: After exercise, a student's heart rate is 128 beats per minute. At rest it was 72 beats per minute. By how much did it increase?
questions.explain: 128 - 72 = 56 beats per minute.

rounds.title: Human Body Systems - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Bones, joints, and muscles support and move the body.

title: Human Body Systems - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: The heart, blood vessels, and lungs transport and exchange gases.

questions.q: What is the main function of the circulatory system?
options: To transport oxygen, nutrients, and wastes around the body
To support the body like a frame
To break down food into nutrients
questions.explain: Blood carries materials to and from every cell in the body.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood AWAY from the heart?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body and lungs.

questions.q: Gas exchange with body cells happens in the tiny vessels called...
questions.explain: Thin-walled capillaries let oxygen, nutrients, and wastes cross into cells.

questions.q: What is the job of red blood cells?
options: Carry oxygen from the lungs to body cells
questions.explain: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

questions.q: What is the job of white blood cells?
questions.explain: White blood cells are part of the immune defense.

questions.q: Platelets in the blood help by...
questions.explain: Platelets plug wounds and start the clotting process.

questions.q: In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen and drops off...
questions.explain: Blood releases carbon dioxide in the alveoli and absorbs oxygen.

questions.q: The tiny air sacs where this gas exchange happens are called...
questions.explain: Alveoli are surrounded by capillaries so gases can diffuse between air and blood.

questions.q: Which muscle makes breathing possible by flattening and pulling the lungs open?
questions.explain: When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, air is drawn into the lungs.

questions.q: Air travels down the windpipe, which is properly called the...
questions.explain: The trachea carries air from the throat toward the lungs.

questions.q: Why does your heart rate increase during exercise?
options: The heart gets tired and slows its pumping strength
Muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, so blood must circulate faster
The lungs stop working during exercise
questions.explain: Faster circulation delivers extra oxygen and removes extra carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which two organ systems work together to deliver oxygen to cells?
questions.explain: The lungs load oxygen into the blood; the circulatory system delivers it.

questions.q: Which term means: a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explain: The term 'artery' means a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
