questions.q: Which term means: a blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart?
questions.explain: The term 'vein' means a blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart.

questions.q: Which term means: a tiny blood vessel where gases and nutrients are exchanged with body cells?
questions.explain: The term 'capillary' means a tiny blood vessel where gases and nutrients are exchanged with body cells.

questions.q: Which term means: tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged?
questions.explain: The term 'alveoli' means tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

questions.q: A student counts 17 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 17 x 4 = 68 beats per minute.

questions.q: A student counts 18 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 18 x 4 = 72 beats per minute.

questions.q: A student counts 16 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 16 x 4 = 64 beats per minute.

questions.q: A heart beats 72 times per minute. How many times does it beat in 5 minutes?
questions.explain: 72 x 5 = 360 beats.

rounds.title: Human Body Systems - Quest 2
rounds.desc: The heart, blood vessels, and lungs transport and exchange gases.

title: Human Body Systems - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Digestion breaks down food; the nervous system controls and coordinates.

questions.q: Where does most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption happen?
questions.explain: The small intestine absorbs most nutrients through its villi.

questions.q: What is the job of the stomach?
options: Churn food and mix it with acid and enzymes to break it down
Absorb most nutrients into the blood
questions.explain: The stomach mechanically churns and chemically digests food.

questions.q: Enzymes in digestion are important because they...
options: kill all bacteria in the body
speed up the chemical breakdown of food
questions.explain: Digestive enzymes break large molecules into small ones that can be absorbed.

questions.q: The tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach is the...
questions.explain: The esophagus moves food to the stomach by muscle contractions (peristalsis).

questions.q: What does the large intestine mainly absorb from the remaining material?
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs water, leaving solid waste.

questions.q: The brain and spinal cord make up the center of which system?
questions.explain: The brain and spinal cord are the control center of the nervous system.

questions.q: Messages travel through the nervous system as...
questions.explain: Neurons transmit electrical impulses quickly throughout the body.

questions.q: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away before you even think about it. This fast, automatic response is...
questions.explain: Reflexes are automatic responses that protect the body quickly.

questions.q: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for thinking, memory, and voluntary actions?
questions.explain: The cerebrum handles thought, memory, and voluntary movement.

questions.q: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and smooth movement?
questions.explain: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and balance.

questions.q: Hormones are chemical messengers that travel through...
questions.explain: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood to reach target organs.

questions.q: When you eat a meal, which systems must cooperate to get glucose to your muscle cells?
questions.explain: Digestion breaks food down; the blood carries glucose to cells.

questions.q: Which term means: the body system that breaks down food and absorbs nutrients?
questions.explain: The term 'digestive system' means the body system that breaks down food and absorbs nutrients.

questions.q: Which term means: the body system of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that controls and coordinates the body?
questions.explain: The term 'nervous system' means the body system of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that controls and coordinates the body.

questions.q: Which term means: a protein that speeds up chemical reactions, such as breaking down food?
questions.explain: The term 'enzyme' means a protein that speeds up chemical reactions, such as breaking down food.

questions.q: Which term means: a nerve cell that carries electrical messages through the body?
questions.explain: The term 'neuron' means a nerve cell that carries electrical messages through the body.

questions.q: A lab group measured breathing rates at rest four times. The measurements are 24, 2, 4, 10 breaths per minute. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

questions.q: A person breathes 14 times per minute at rest. How many breaths is that in 10 minutes?
questions.explain: 14 x 10 = 140 breaths.

questions.q: During digestion practice, a model stomach 'churns' 6 times in 30 seconds. How many churns is that per minute?
questions.explain: 6 churns in half a minute = 12 per minute.

questions.q: A nerve signal travels 240 meters in 2 seconds. What is its average speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 240 / 2 = 120 meters per second.

rounds.title: Human Body Systems - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Digestion breaks down food; the nervous system controls and coordinates.

title: Human Body Systems - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: immune defense and how body systems work together.

questions.q: The first line of defense of the immune system includes...
options: white blood cells in the heart only
skin and mucus that block pathogens from entering
questions.explain: Barriers like skin and mucus keep most pathogens out.

questions.q: How do vaccines protect the body?
options: They kill every microbe in the body permanently
They train the immune system to recognize a pathogen so it can respond faster later
questions.explain: Vaccines expose the immune system to a safe form of a pathogen so memory cells form.

questions.q: Antibodies are special because they...
options: match and help destroy specific pathogens
questions.explain: Each antibody fits a particular pathogen and marks it for destruction.

questions.q: Why do you usually get diseases like chickenpox only once?
options: Antibiotics stay in your body forever
Memory cells in the immune system recognize the pathogen and respond quickly the second time
questions.explain: Immune memory makes the second response fast enough to prevent illness.

questions.q: A fever during an illness is the body...
options: raising its temperature to make conditions harder for many pathogens
questions.explain: A moderate fever can slow pathogen growth and speed immune responses.

questions.q: Which cells are the 'soldiers' that seek out and destroy pathogens in the blood?
questions.explain: White blood cells patrol the body and attack invaders.

questions.q: When you get a cut, several systems respond. Which sequence is correct?
options: The lungs send oxygen directly through the cut
Platelets clot the blood, white blood cells fight germs, and skin cells divide to close the wound
Muscles grow over the cut immediately
Neurons digest the germs, then bones cover the wound
questions.explain: Clotting, immune defense, and cell division (mitosis) repair a cut together.

questions.q: Homeostasis in the body means...
options: keeping internal conditions like temperature and blood sugar steady
questions.explain: Body systems cooperate to keep internal conditions stable.

questions.q: When you are too hot, your body sweats and blood vessels widen. This is an example of...
options: the immune system fighting a virus
the nervous and circulatory systems maintaining homeostasis
questions.explain: Sweating and increased blood flow to the skin release heat and restore balance.

questions.q: Which organ acts like a filter that removes wastes and old cells from the blood?
options: the liver (along with the kidneys for urine wastes)
questions.explain: The liver filters blood and processes wastes; the kidneys filter blood to make urine.

questions.q: Diabetes involves a problem with the hormone insulin, which normally controls...
questions.explain: Insulin helps cells take in glucose and keeps blood sugar steady.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the body is organized into interacting systems instead of one single system doing everything?
options: Different systems specialize, and their cooperation keeps the whole body alive
One system would be too small to see
questions.explain: Specialized systems depend on each other; failure in one affects the rest.

questions.q: Which term means: the body system that defends against pathogens and disease?
questions.explain: The term 'immune system' means the body system that defends against pathogens and disease.

questions.q: Which term means: anything that causes disease, such as certain bacteria and viruses?
questions.explain: The term 'pathogen' means anything that causes disease, such as certain bacteria and viruses.

questions.q: Which term means: a protein made by the immune system that helps destroy specific pathogens?
questions.explain: The term 'antibody' means a protein made by the immune system that helps destroy specific pathogens.

questions.q: Which term means: a substance that trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen before real infection?
questions.explain: The term 'vaccine' means a substance that trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen before real infection.

questions.q: A student counts 21 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply the 15-second count by 4: 21 x 4 = 84 beats per minute.

questions.q: A doctor counts a pulse of 19 beats in 15 seconds at rest and 30 beats in 15 seconds after running. What are the two heart rates in beats per minute?
questions.explain: Multiply each 15-second count by 4: 19 x 4 = 76 and 30 x 4 = 120.

questions.q: A class measured resting pulse rates for a student on four days. The measurements are 7, 30, 12, 19 beats per minute. What is the average?
questions.explain: Add the values and divide by the number of measurements (4).

questions.q: Your body has about 5 liters of blood, and the heart pumps about 5 liters per minute at rest. About how many liters does it pump in 12 minutes at rest?
questions.explain: 5 liters per minute x 12 minutes = 60 liters.

rounds.title: Human Body Systems - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: immune defense and how body systems work together.

title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Biotic and abiotic factors, populations, habitats, and limiting factors.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY abiotic factors?
questions.explain: Abiotic factors are nonliving: sunlight, water, temperature, and soil.

questions.q: Which of these is a biotic factor in a pond ecosystem?
questions.explain: Algae are living organisms, so they are a biotic factor.

questions.q: All the members of one species living in an area make up a...
questions.explain: A population is all individuals of one species in an area.

questions.q: How is a community different from an ecosystem?
options: A community is always larger than an ecosystem
A community is only the living things; an ecosystem also includes nonliving factors
questions.explain: An ecosystem = community (living) + abiotic (nonliving) factors interacting.

questions.q: The place where an organism lives and finds food, water, and shelter is its...
questions.explain: A habitat is the environment that meets an organism's needs.

questions.q: An organism's niche is best described as...
options: its role or job in the ecosystem, including what it eats and how it behaves
the exact hole it sleeps in
the number of offspring it has
questions.explain: A niche is the organism's functional role in its community.

questions.q: Which factor would be a limiting factor for a population of plants in a desert?
questions.explain: Limiting factors restrict population growth; in a desert, water is scarce.

questions.q: Two male deer fighting over a mate is an example of...
questions.explain: Members of the same species competing for mates or resources is intraspecific competition.

questions.q: Which change would most likely INCREASE the carrying capacity of a forest for deer?
options: more wolves moving into the forest
an increase in the grasses and shrubs that deer eat
questions.explain: More food resources allow the environment to support more deer.

questions.q: A scientist studies how rain affects the growth of moss on a forest floor. The rain is which part of the ecosystem?
questions.explain: Rain is nonliving, so it is an abiotic factor.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders ecological organization from smallest to largest?
questions.explain: One organism joins its population; populations form a community; community plus abiotic factors form an ecosystem.

questions.q: Bees pollinating flowers while collecting nectar is an interaction between...
options: a biotic and a chemical factor only
questions.explain: Both the bees and the flowers are living things: biotic factors.

questions.q: Which term means: all the living and nonliving things that interact in an area?
questions.explain: The term 'ecosystem' means all the living and nonliving things that interact in an area.

questions.q: Which term means: a living part of an ecosystem, such as a plant, an animal, or a bacterium?
questions.explain: The term 'biotic factor' means a living part of an ecosystem, such as a plant, an animal, or a bacterium.

questions.q: What does the term 'abiotic factor' mean?
options: a nonliving part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, water, or temperature
the natural environment where an organism lives and meets its needs
an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms
a diagram showing how available energy decreases at each higher feeding level
questions.explain: 'Abiotic factor' means a nonliving part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, water, or temperature.

questions.q: Which term means: the natural environment where an organism lives and meets its needs?
questions.explain: The term 'habitat' means the natural environment where an organism lives and meets its needs.

questions.q: Scientists count 12 frogs in a pond study plot covering 6 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.explain: Population density = count / area = 12 / 6 = 2 per square meter.

questions.q: Scientists count 18 dandelions in a field plot covering 3 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.explain: Population density = count / area = 18 / 3 = 6 per square meter.

questions.q: Scientists count 80 dandelions in a field plot covering 10 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.explain: Population density = count / area = 80 / 10 = 8 per square meter.

questions.q: Scientists count 12 dandelions in a field plot covering 4 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.explain: Population density = count / area = 12 / 4 = 3 per square meter.

rounds.title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Biotic and abiotic factors, populations, habitats, and limiting factors.

title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Food chains, food webs, and the 10 percent rule of energy transfer.

questions.q: In a food chain, the arrows point in the direction of...
options: energy flow, from the organism being eaten to the eater
questions.explain: Arrows show energy moving from food to the organism that eats it.

questions.q: Why does an energy pyramid get narrower toward the top?
options: Energy is created fresh at each level
About 90 percent of energy is lost at each level, mostly as heat and life processes
Producers give away their energy to the soil
questions.explain: Only about 10 percent of energy transfers upward, so less is available at higher levels.

questions.q: If all the producers in an ecosystem were removed, what would happen first?
options: Decomposers would start making food from sunlight
Herbivores would run out of food and their populations would fall
Nothing would change for the other organisms
questions.explain: All food chains start with producers; removing them starves herbivores first.

questions.q: A rabbit that eats grass is classified as a...
questions.explain: Rabbits eat producers (grass), making them primary consumers and herbivores.

questions.q: A hawk that eats a snake that ate a mouse that ate grass seeds sits at which level?
questions.explain: Grass -> mouse (primary) -> snake (secondary) -> hawk (tertiary).

questions.q: Why are there usually fewer top predators than herbivores in an ecosystem?
options: Less energy reaches the top levels, so the ecosystem can support fewer top predators
Top predators do not need food
questions.explain: With only about 10 percent of energy passed up each level, few predators can be supported.

questions.q: Decomposers are essential to food webs because they...
options: break down dead organisms and return nutrients to the soil for producers
questions.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients so producers can grow.

questions.q: Which organism is a producer?
questions.explain: Oak trees make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers.

questions.q: A food web is more realistic than a single food chain because...
options: most organisms eat and are eaten by many different species
questions.explain: Real feeding relationships form an interconnected web, not one straight line.

questions.q: A bear that eats both berries and fish is classified as an...
questions.explain: Omnivores eat both plants and animals.

questions.q: Where does the energy in a food chain originally come from?
options: the Sun, captured by producers in photosynthesis
questions.explain: Producers convert sunlight into stored chemical energy that flows through the web.

questions.q: If the mouse population suddenly crashes, the most likely effect on owls that eat mice is...
options: owls will have less food and their population may decrease
questions.explain: Losing a main prey species reduces the food available to its predators.

questions.q: Which term means: an organism that makes its own food, usually through photosynthesis?
questions.explain: The term 'producer' means an organism that makes its own food, usually through photosynthesis.

questions.q: Which term means: an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms?
questions.explain: The term 'consumer' means an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms.

questions.q: Which term means: the network of overlapping food chains in an ecosystem?
questions.explain: The term 'food web' means the network of overlapping food chains in an ecosystem.

questions.q: What does the term 'energy pyramid' mean?
options: a consumer that eats only other animals
a living part of an ecosystem, such as a plant, an animal, or a bacterium
a nonliving part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, water, or temperature
a diagram showing how available energy decreases at each higher feeding level
questions.explain: 'Energy pyramid' means a diagram showing how available energy decreases at each higher feeding level.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 10000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the primary consumers (herbivores)?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 10000 / 10 = 1000 kilocalories.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 20000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 20000 / 100 = 200 kilocalories.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 100000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 100000 / 100 = 1000 kilocalories.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 40000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the primary consumers (herbivores)?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 40000 / 10 = 4000 kilocalories.

rounds.title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Food chains, food webs, and the 10 percent rule of energy transfer.

title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Symbiosis, competition, predator-prey cycles, and carrying capacity.

questions.q: A bee drinks nectar from a flower and carries pollen to other flowers. Both the bee and the plant benefit. This relationship is...
questions.explain: Both species benefit, so it is mutualism.

questions.q: A tick feeds on a dog's blood, weakening the dog. This relationship is...
questions.explain: The tick benefits while the dog is harmed: parasitism.

questions.q: Barnacles attach to a whale and filter food from the water. The whale is not helped or harmed. This is...
questions.explain: One benefits and the other is unaffected: commensalism.

questions.q: Two plants growing close together both receive less light and water. This is an example of...
questions.explain: Both plants struggle for the same limited resources: competition.

questions.q: In a predator-prey cycle, when prey numbers rise, what usually happens next?
options: Predator numbers rise because more food is available
Predator numbers immediately fall to zero
questions.explain: More prey supports more predators, whose numbers then increase (with a time lag).

questions.q: After predator numbers rise, prey numbers usually...
options: fall, because more prey are being eaten
questions.explain: More predators eat more prey, so the prey population declines.

questions.q: An invasive plant species spreads quickly and shades out native seedlings. Its main effect is...
options: increasing competition for light, which can reduce native plant populations
questions.explain: Invasive species compete for resources and can crowd out natives.

questions.q: A graph of a deer population rises for several years, then levels off and stays fairly steady. The leveling off most likely means...
options: all the predators moved in at once
the population reached the carrying capacity of the environment
questions.explain: Populations level off at carrying capacity when limiting factors balance births.

questions.q: Which is an example of a predator-prey pair?
options: oak tree and squirrel eating acorns only for storage
questions.explain: Foxes hunt and eat rabbits: predator and prey. (Squirrel-acorn is also eating, but the classic hunt relationship here is fox-rabbit.)

questions.q: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. The fish get protection, and the anemone gets scraps of food and defense from the fish. This is...
questions.explain: Both the clownfish and the anemone benefit: mutualism.

questions.q: Which human action would most likely REDUCE competition stress on a wildlife population?
questions.explain: More habitat means more food and space, easing competition.

questions.q: Mistletoe grows on tree branches and absorbs water and nutrients from the tree, weakening it. Mistletoe is a...
questions.explain: Mistletoe benefits at the tree's expense, making it a parasite.

questions.q: Which term means: a relationship in which both species benefit?
questions.explain: The term 'mutualism' means a relationship in which both species benefit.

questions.q: Which term means: a relationship in which one species benefits and the other is harmed?
questions.explain: The term 'parasitism' means a relationship in which one species benefits and the other is harmed.

questions.q: Which term means: the struggle between organisms for limited resources such as food, water, or space?
questions.explain: The term 'competition' means the struggle between organisms for limited resources such as food, water, or space.

questions.q: What does the term 'carrying capacity' mean?
options: the largest number of individuals of a species that an environment can support over time
a diagram showing how available energy decreases at each higher feeding level
an organism that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil
the continuous movement of carbon between living things, the air, water, and rocks
questions.explain: 'Carrying capacity' means the largest number of individuals of a species that an environment can support over time.

questions.q: A population of rabbits starts at 800 individuals and grows by 20% in one year. How many individuals are there after the year?
A population of frogs starts at 400 individuals and grows by 20% in one year. How many individuals are there after the year?
A population of deer starts at 500 individuals and grows by 25% in one year. How many individuals are there after the year?
A population of deer starts at 200 individuals and grows by 25% in one year. How many individuals are there after the year?

rounds.title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Symbiosis, competition, predator-prey cycles, and carrying capacity.

title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: carbon and water cycles, and human impacts on ecosystems.

questions.q: How does carbon return to the atmosphere from living things?
options: Animals bury carbon in rocks instantly
Cellular respiration by organisms and decomposition release carbon dioxide
Plants store carbon forever with no release
questions.explain: Respiration and decay release CO2 back into the air.

questions.q: How do plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
options: By absorbing it through their roots only
They do not interact with carbon dioxide
By taking it in for photosynthesis
questions.explain: Photosynthesis pulls CO2 from the air to build glucose.

questions.q: Burning fossil fuels affects the carbon cycle by...
options: releasing stored carbon into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide faster than natural processes remove it
removing carbon dioxide from the air
questions.explain: Combustion frees long-stored carbon as CO2, adding to atmospheric levels.

questions.q: In the water cycle, water vapor in the air cools and changes back into liquid droplets, forming clouds. This step is...
questions.explain: Condensation is gas changing to liquid, forming cloud droplets.

questions.q: Water released from plant leaves into the air is called...
questions.explain: Plants lose water vapor through leaf openings in transpiration.

questions.q: Why are nitrogen-fixing bacteria important for plants?
options: They produce nitrogen gas for animals to breathe
They convert nitrogen from the air into forms plants can absorb from the soil
questions.explain: Most plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; these bacteria 'fix' it into usable compounds.

questions.q: Excess fertilizer runs off a farm into a lake. Algae bloom, die, and decay uses up oxygen. The most likely result is...
options: fish and other aquatic animals may die from low oxygen
questions.explain: Decomposing algae blooms consume oxygen, creating dead zones for aquatic life.

questions.q: Which action best helps maintain biodiversity?
options: Removing all predators from an area
Replacing forests with one crop species
Protecting a variety of habitats from destruction
questions.explain: Varied, protected habitats support many species and keep ecosystems resilient.

questions.q: A resource that nature replaces at about the rate it is used, like timber from a replanted forest, is...
questions.explain: Renewable resources regenerate on a human timescale when managed well.

questions.q: Which of these is a NONRENEWABLE resource?
questions.explain: Coal formed over millions of years and cannot be replaced quickly.

questions.q: Composting food scraps helps ecosystems because...
options: decomposers turn the scraps into nutrients that enrich the soil
it removes the need for producers
scraps become fossil fuels in weeks
questions.explain: Decomposition recycles nutrients from waste back into soil.

questions.q: If a disease kills most of the frogs in a pond, the insect population that frogs eat will most likely...
options: increase, because fewer predators are eating them
questions.explain: Removing a predator releases its prey population from predation pressure.

questions.q: Which term means: an organism that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil?
questions.explain: The term 'decomposer' means an organism that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil.

questions.q: Which term means: the continuous movement of carbon between living things, the air, water, and rocks?
questions.explain: The term 'carbon cycle' means the continuous movement of carbon between living things, the air, water, and rocks.

questions.q: Which term means: an organism that hunts and eats other animals?
questions.explain: The term 'predator' means an organism that hunts and eats other animals.

questions.q: What does the term 'prey' mean?
options: the continuous movement of carbon between living things, the air, water, and rocks
the struggle between organisms for limited resources such as food, water, or space
an organism that is hunted and eaten by a predator
an organism that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil
questions.explain: 'Prey' means an organism that is hunted and eaten by a predator.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 10000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the tertiary consumers?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 10000 / 1000 = 10 kilocalories.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem store 50000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the primary consumers (herbivores)?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy moves to the next level: 50000 / 10 = 5000 kilocalories.

questions.q: A population of rabbits starts at 400 individuals and decreases by 10% in one year. How many individuals remain?
A population of deer starts at 500 individuals and decreases by 10% in one year. How many individuals remain?

rounds.title: Ecosystems & Energy Flow - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: carbon and water cycles, and human impacts on ecosystems.

title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: States of matter, particle motion, and physical properties.

questions.q: Which statement about the particles in a gas is correct?
options: They move fast and spread out to fill their container
They do not move at all
They slide past each other but keep a fixed volume
They are locked in a fixed pattern
questions.explain: Gas particles move rapidly and expand to fill any container.

questions.q: A liquid has...
options: a definite shape and a definite volume
no definite volume and no definite shape
a definite volume but takes the shape of its container
questions.explain: Liquids keep their volume but flow into the shape of their container.

questions.q: When a solid is heated and its particles move faster and spread slightly, the solid usually...
questions.explain: Heating increases particle motion, causing thermal expansion.

questions.q: Ice melting into water is caused by...
options: a chemical reaction with the air
the water molecules splitting into atoms
the particles gaining energy and breaking out of their fixed positions
questions.explain: Melting happens when particles gain enough energy to move more freely.

questions.q: Dew forming on grass on a cool morning is an example of...
questions.explain: Water vapor in the air condenses into liquid on cool surfaces.

questions.q: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) disappears without leaving a puddle. It changes directly from a solid to a gas. This is called...
questions.explain: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas.

questions.q: Which of these is a physical property of a substance?
questions.explain: Density is a physical property; rusting and burning describe chemical behavior.

questions.q: Mass and weight are different because...
options: they are measured with the same instrument
mass is the amount of matter, while weight depends on gravity
mass changes when you go to the Moon
questions.explain: Mass stays constant; weight changes with gravity (less on the Moon).

questions.q: A sealed bottle of water is placed in a freezer. After the water freezes, the bottle bulges. Why?
options: Water expands as it freezes, taking up more volume
questions.explain: Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes.

questions.q: Which state of matter has particles arranged in a tight, regular pattern that vibrate in place?
questions.explain: Solid particles are packed in a fixed arrangement and vibrate in place.

questions.q: Boiling differs from evaporation because boiling...
options: happens throughout the liquid at a specific temperature
questions.explain: Evaporation occurs at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout at the boiling point.

questions.q: As the temperature of a gas in a sealed, rigid container increases, the pressure inside...
options: increases, because particles hit the walls harder and more often
questions.explain: Faster particles collide more forcefully, raising pressure in a fixed volume.

questions.q: Which term means: anything that has mass and takes up space?
questions.explain: The term 'matter' means anything that has mass and takes up space.

questions.q: Which term means: the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid?
questions.explain: The term 'melting point' means the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.

questions.q: Which term means: the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid?
questions.explain: The term 'boiling point' means the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid.

questions.q: Which term means: a change that alters the form of a substance but not its chemical identity?
questions.explain: The term 'physical change' means a change that alters the form of a substance but not its chemical identity.

questions.q: A rectangular block is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 6 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explain: Volume = length x width x height = 5 x 4 x 6 = 120 cubic centimeters.

questions.q: A rectangular block is 2 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 5 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explain: Volume = length x width x height = 2 x 4 x 5 = 40 cubic centimeters.

questions.q: A metal block has a mass of 50 grams and a volume of 5 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume = 50 / 5 = 10 grams per cubic centimeter.

questions.q: A rock sample has a mass of 6 grams and a volume of 6 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume = 6 / 6 = 1 grams per cubic centimeter.

rounds.title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 1
rounds.desc: States of matter, particle motion, and physical properties.

title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Atoms, elements, atomic number, and the periodic table.

questions.q: The nucleus of an atom contains...
questions.explain: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons move around it.

questions.q: What determines which element an atom is?
options: the number of protons in its nucleus
the number of electrons it can lose
questions.explain: The atomic number (proton count) defines the element.

questions.q: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals...
questions.explain: Equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons make the atom neutral.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.explain: Gold's symbol Au comes from its Latin name, aurum. (Ag is silver.)

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explain: Sodium's symbol Na comes from natrium. (S is sulfur.)

questions.q: Oxygen has an atomic number of 8. How many protons does an oxygen atom have?
questions.explain: The atomic number equals the number of protons: 8.

questions.q: Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table...
options: were discovered in the same year
questions.explain: Group members share similar properties because of similar electron arrangements.

questions.q: Most elements on the periodic table are...
options: metals, found on the left and in the middle
nonmetals, found on the right only
questions.explain: Metals make up the majority of elements and sit on the left/center of the table.

questions.q: A molecule of oxygen gas is written O2. Is O2 an element or a compound?
options: It is a compound, because it has two atoms
It is an element, because it contains only one kind of atom
questions.explain: Compounds need two or more DIFFERENT elements; O2 has only oxygen atoms.

questions.q: Water (H2O) is a compound because...
options: it is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
questions.explain: Compounds combine different elements in fixed ratios with new properties.

questions.q: Which particle has a negative electric charge?
questions.explain: Electrons carry a negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons are neutral.

questions.q: An atom's mass number is the total number of...
questions.explain: Mass number counts the heavy particles in the nucleus: protons + neutrons.

questions.q: Which term means: the smallest unit of an element that still has the properties of that element?
questions.explain: The term 'atom' means the smallest unit of an element that still has the properties of that element.

questions.q: Which term means: a pure substance made of only one kind of atom?
questions.explain: The term 'element' means a pure substance made of only one kind of atom.

questions.q: Which term means: a positively charged particle found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The term 'proton' means a positively charged particle found in the nucleus of an atom.

questions.q: What does the term 'atomic number' mean?
options: the substance that is dissolved in a solution
the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it identifies the element
a material that allows heat or electricity to flow through it easily
the mass of a substance divided by its volume
questions.explain: 'Atomic number' means the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it identifies the element.

questions.q: An atom of sulfur has an atomic number of 16 and a mass number of 32. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 32 - 16 = 16.

questions.q: An atom of sodium has an atomic number of 11 and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.q: An atom of nitrogen has an atomic number of 7 and a mass number of 14. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 14 - 7 = 7.

questions.q: An atom of oxygen has an atomic number of 8 and a mass number of 16. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 16 - 8 = 8.

rounds.title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Atoms, elements, atomic number, and the periodic table.

title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Compounds, mixtures, solutions, and ways to separate them.

questions.q: Which method would best separate a mixture of sand and water?
questions.explain: Filtration traps the solid sand while water passes through.

questions.q: Iron filings are mixed into sand. The fastest way to remove the iron is to...
options: drag a magnet through the mixture
heat the mixture until it melts
questions.explain: Iron is magnetic; the magnet pulls it out without affecting the sand.

questions.q: To recover salt that has been dissolved in water, you can...
options: evaporate the water, leaving the salt behind
questions.explain: Dissolved salt passes through filters, but evaporation removes the water and leaves the salt.

questions.q: In a glass of lemonade, the sugar that disappears into the water is the...
questions.explain: The solute is the substance that gets dissolved.

questions.q: In the lemonade, the water is the...
questions.explain: The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving.

questions.q: Brass is made by combining copper and zinc metals that are not chemically bonded. Brass is a...
options: mixture (a solid solution called an alloy)
questions.explain: Alloys are mixtures of metals; their parts are not chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.

questions.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
options: a bowl of mixed nuts and raisins
questions.explain: Trail mix is unevenly mixed, so it is heterogeneous; salt water and air are uniform (homogeneous).

questions.q: Which change would make sugar dissolve FASTER in tea?
options: adding the sugar all in one clump and leaving it still
using one large sugar cube instead of granules, without stirring
questions.explain: Stirring spreads the solute through the solvent faster.

questions.q: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at a given temperature is called...
questions.explain: A saturated solution holds the maximum dissolved solute at that temperature.

questions.q: Solution A has 5 grams of sugar in 100 milliliters of water. Solution B has 20 grams in 100 milliliters. Which is more concentrated?
questions.explain: More solute in the same amount of solvent means a higher concentration.

questions.q: Air is best classified as...
options: a mixture of gases (mostly nitrogen and oxygen)
questions.explain: Air's gases are physically mixed, not chemically bonded.

questions.q: Why can the parts of a mixture be separated by physical means?
options: Because mixtures have only one substance
Because mixtures are smaller than compounds
Because the substances are not chemically bonded and keep their own properties
questions.explain: Without chemical bonds, differences in properties (size, magnetism, boiling point) allow separation.

questions.q: Which term means: a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio?
questions.explain: The term 'compound' means a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.

questions.q: Which term means: a combination of two or more substances that can be separated by physical means?
questions.explain: The term 'mixture' means a combination of two or more substances that can be separated by physical means.

questions.q: Which term means: a mixture in which one substance dissolves evenly into another?
questions.explain: The term 'solution' means a mixture in which one substance dissolves evenly into another.

questions.q: What does the term 'solvent' mean?
options: the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid
a process in which substances are rearranged to form new substances
the principle that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
the substance that does the dissolving in a solution
questions.explain: 'Solvent' means the substance that does the dissolving in a solution.

questions.q: A solution is made by dissolving 30 grams of salt in water to make 200 grams of salt solution. What is the percent concentration by mass?
questions.explain: Percent = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100 = (30 / 200) x 100 = 15 percent.

questions.q: A solution is made by dissolving 25 grams of salt in water to make 250 grams of salt solution. What is the percent concentration by mass?
questions.explain: Percent = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100 = (25 / 250) x 100 = 10 percent.

questions.q: At a certain temperature, 36 grams of a salt dissolve completely in 100 milliliters of water. At the same temperature, how much salt dissolves in 300 milliliters of water?
questions.explain: The amount scales with the water: 36 x 3 = 108 grams.

questions.q: A student mixes 15 grams of drink powder into 150 grams of water. What is the total mass of the solution?
questions.explain: Mass adds up: 15 + 150 = 165 grams.

rounds.title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Compounds, mixtures, solutions, and ways to separate them.

title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: chemical reactions, conservation of mass, and density.

questions.q: Which of these is the clearest sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
options: A new substance with different properties forms, such as a gas from mixing two liquids
A solid melts into a liquid
questions.explain: Formation of a new substance (with clues like gas, color change, or a precipitate) signals a chemical change.

questions.q: Baking soda fizzes when vinegar is added because...
options: air escapes from the powder's holes
a chemical reaction produces carbon dioxide gas
questions.explain: The acid and baking soda react to form carbon dioxide bubbles.

questions.q: Burning wood is a chemical change because...
options: the wood is converted into new substances: ash, smoke, and gases
questions.explain: Burning creates new substances, so it is a chemical change.

questions.q: Which of these is a PHYSICAL change?
questions.explain: Tearing changes only the paper's shape; it is still paper. The others create new substances.

questions.q: An iron nail left outside turns orange-brown and flaky. This rusting is a...
options: chemical change, because a new substance (rust) forms
physical change, because only the color changed
questions.explain: Rust is a new substance (iron oxide), so rusting is chemical.

questions.q: In the reaction 'hydrogen + oxygen -> water', the reactants are...
questions.explain: Reactants are the starting substances on the left side of the arrow.

questions.q: A student burns a candle completely inside a sealed jar on a balance. The total mass stays the same. This demonstrates...
options: the law of conservation of mass
questions.explain: In a closed system, atoms are rearranged but mass is conserved.

questions.q: If 10 grams of wax burn and react with 26 grams of oxygen in a sealed container, how many grams of products form?
questions.explain: Conservation of mass: 10 + 26 = 36 grams of products.

questions.q: Why do some reactions speed up when heated?
options: Higher temperature makes particles move faster and collide more often with more energy
questions.explain: More frequent, more energetic collisions speed up reactions.

questions.q: Crushing a solid reactant into powder speeds up its reaction because...
options: more surface area is exposed for collisions
questions.explain: Greater surface area gives particles more contact, speeding the reaction.

questions.q: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings (the container feels warm) is called...
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions release energy, usually as heat.

questions.q: An instant cold pack feels cold because the reaction inside...
options: releases heat into the pack only
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions absorb heat, making surroundings feel colder.

questions.q: Which term means: a change that produces one or more new substances?
questions.explain: The term 'chemical change' means a change that produces one or more new substances.

questions.q: Which term means: a process in which substances are rearranged to form new substances?
questions.explain: The term 'chemical reaction' means a process in which substances are rearranged to form new substances.

questions.q: Which term means: the principle that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction?
questions.explain: The term 'conservation of mass' means the principle that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

questions.q: What does the term 'density' mean?
options: a positively charged particle found in the nucleus of an atom
a pure substance made of only one kind of atom
the mass of a substance divided by its volume
a negatively charged particle that moves around the nucleus of an atom
questions.explain: 'Density' means the mass of a substance divided by its volume.

questions.q: A rock sample has a mass of 80 grams and a volume of 10 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume = 80 / 10 = 8 grams per cubic centimeter.

questions.q: A liquid sample has a mass of 50 grams and a volume of 5 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume = 50 / 5 = 10 grams per cubic centimeter.

questions.q: A liquid sample has a mass of 75 grams and a volume of 25 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume = 75 / 25 = 3 grams per cubic centimeter.

questions.q: A block has a density of 5 grams per cubic centimeter and a volume of 6 cubic centimeters. What is its mass?
questions.explain: Mass = density x volume = 5 x 6 = 30 grams.

rounds.title: Matter & Chemistry Basics - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: chemical reactions, conservation of mass, and density.

title: Forces & Motion - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, and reading motion graphs.

questions.q: To describe an object's motion, you must compare its position to a...
questions.explain: Motion is judged by change in position relative to a reference point.

questions.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
options: Speed includes a direction; velocity does not
They are measured in different base units only
Velocity includes a direction; speed does not
questions.explain: Velocity is speed in a stated direction, like 10 meters per second north.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, a horizontal (flat) line means the object is...
questions.explain: If distance does not change over time, the object is at rest.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, a steeper upward slope means...
questions.explain: Slope on a distance-time graph equals speed; steeper means faster.

questions.q: A student walks 100 meters in 25 seconds, stops for 10 seconds, then walks back. In a distance-time graph of the first part, the slope represents...
options: the student's speed of 4 meters per second
questions.explain: Slope = distance/time = 100/25 = 4 meters per second.

questions.q: Which is an example of velocity?
options: A runner who finished in 12 seconds
A car parked at a rest stop
A plane flying 250 meters per second toward the northeast
A plane flying 250 meters per second
questions.explain: Velocity must state both speed and direction.

questions.q: A car travels at a constant 60 kilometers per hour for 2 hours. How far does it go?
questions.explain: Distance = speed x time = 60 x 2 = 120 kilometers.

questions.q: Acceleration happens whenever an object...
options: speeds up, slows down, or changes direction
moves at a constant speed in a straight line
questions.explain: Any change in velocity - including direction - is acceleration.

questions.q: A bike rounds a curve at a constant speed of 8 meters per second. Is the bike accelerating?
options: No, because its speed is constant
Yes, because its speed is increasing
Yes, because its direction is changing
questions.explain: Changing direction changes velocity, so the bike is accelerating.

questions.q: Which unit pair is correct for speed in SI units?
questions.explain: SI speed is measured in meters per second.

questions.q: A bus travels 90 kilometers in 1.5 hours. Its average speed is...
questions.explain: Average speed = total distance / total time = 90 / 1.5 = 60 km/h.

questions.q: What does an object's position tell you?
options: Where it is compared to a reference point
How fast it will move later
questions.explain: Position is a location relative to a chosen reference point.

questions.q: Which term means: the distance an object travels divided by the time it takes to travel that distance?
questions.explain: The term 'speed' means the distance an object travels divided by the time it takes to travel that distance.

questions.q: Which term means: the speed of an object in a specific direction?
questions.explain: The term 'velocity' means the speed of an object in a specific direction.

questions.q: Which term means: the rate at which an object's velocity changes over time?
questions.explain: The term 'acceleration' means the rate at which an object's velocity changes over time.

questions.q: Which term means: a place or object used for comparison to determine whether an object is in motion?
questions.explain: The term 'reference point' means a place or object used for comparison to determine whether an object is in motion.

questions.q: A toy car travels 40 meters in 5 seconds at a constant speed. What is the speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 40 / 5 = 8 meters per second.

questions.q: A cyclist travels 15 meters in 5 seconds at a constant speed. What is the speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 15 / 5 = 3 meters per second.

questions.q: A cyclist travels 60 meters in 6 seconds at a constant speed. What is the speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 60 / 6 = 10 meters per second.

questions.q: A skateboarder travels 36 meters in 3 seconds at a constant speed. What is the speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 36 / 3 = 12 meters per second.

rounds.title: Forces & Motion - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Speed, velocity, acceleration, and reading motion graphs.

title: Forces & Motion - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, and gravity.

questions.q: A book sits motionless on a table. The forces on the book are...
options: balanced - gravity pulls down and the table pushes up with equal force
only gravity, since tables cannot push
absent, because the book is not moving
questions.explain: Equal and opposite forces cancel, so the book's motion does not change.

questions.q: Which action reduces friction between a sled and snow?
options: smoothing and waxing the bottom of the sled
questions.explain: Smoother surfaces and wax lower the friction between sled and snow.

questions.q: Friction is helpful when...
options: the tread of your shoes grips the floor so you can walk without slipping
it makes a machine's parts overheat
it slows a rolling ball you wanted to keep moving
questions.explain: Friction between shoes and the ground makes walking possible.

questions.q: The strength of gravity between two objects depends on...
options: their masses and the distance between them
questions.explain: More mass means stronger gravity; greater distance weakens it.

questions.q: Why does an astronaut weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
options: The Moon has no gravity at all
The Moon has less mass, so its gravity pulls with less force
Spacesuits are lighter on the Moon
questions.explain: Weight is the force of gravity; the Moon's smaller mass pulls less.

questions.q: A falling leaf flutters slowly while a falling acorn drops quickly, mainly because of...
options: air resistance acting on the leaf's large surface
questions.explain: Air resistance (a form of friction) opposes the leaf's fall more strongly.

questions.q: If the net force on a moving object is zero, the object will...
options: keep moving at a constant velocity
questions.explain: With balanced forces, motion does not change (Newton's first law).

questions.q: A spring scale measures force by...
options: how much a spring stretches when a force pulls on it, read in newtons
questions.explain: Spring stretch is proportional to force and is read in newtons.

questions.q: Which surface would create the MOST sliding friction for a wooden block?
questions.explain: Rougher surfaces generate more friction.

questions.q: Rolling friction is usually ______ than sliding friction, which is why wheels are useful.
questions.explain: Rolling friction is weaker than sliding friction, so wheels reduce effort.

questions.q: Two magnets repel each other without touching. This shows that forces can...
options: act at a distance without direct contact
questions.explain: Gravity and magnetism are non-contact forces that act at a distance.

questions.q: A soccer ball rolling on grass eventually stops because...
options: friction acts in the opposite direction of its motion
the ball runs out of velocity
questions.explain: Friction opposes the motion and slows the ball to a stop.

questions.q: Which term means: a push or a pull exerted on an object?
questions.explain: The term 'force' means a push or a pull exerted on an object.

questions.q: Which term means: a force that opposes motion between two surfaces that are touching?
questions.explain: The term 'friction' means a force that opposes motion between two surfaces that are touching.

questions.q: Which term means: the attractive force between any two objects that have mass?
questions.explain: The term 'gravity' means the attractive force between any two objects that have mass.

questions.q: Which term means: the overall force acting on an object after all individual forces are combined?
questions.explain: The term 'net force' means the overall force acting on an object after all individual forces are combined.

questions.q: Two students push a box in the same direction with forces of 15 newtons and 30 newtons. What is the net force on the box?
questions.explain: Forces in the same direction add: 15 + 30 = 45 newtons.

questions.q: In a tug-of-war, one team pulls with 10 newtons and the other team pulls the opposite way with 15 newtons. What is the magnitude of the net force?
questions.explain: Forces in opposite directions subtract: |10 - 15| = 5 newtons.

questions.q: Two students push a box in the same direction with forces of 50 newtons and 5 newtons. What is the net force on the box?
questions.explain: Forces in the same direction add: 50 + 5 = 55 newtons.

questions.q: In a tug-of-war, one team pulls with 50 newtons and the other team pulls the opposite way with 15 newtons. What is the magnitude of the net force?
questions.explain: Forces in opposite directions subtract: |50 - 15| = 35 newtons.

rounds.title: Forces & Motion - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, and gravity.

title: Forces & Motion - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Newton's three laws of motion in everyday situations.

questions.q: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly. This is best explained by...
options: friction between the seat and passenger
inertia - the passenger's body tends to keep moving forward
questions.explain: Newton's first law: objects in motion stay in motion unless a force acts.

questions.q: Which object has the most inertia?
questions.explain: Inertia increases with mass; the massive truck resists changes in motion most.

questions.q: According to Newton's second law, applying the same force to a bowling ball and a tennis ball, the tennis ball will...
options: accelerate much more, because it has less mass
questions.explain: a = F/m: smaller mass gives greater acceleration for the same force.

questions.q: To give a heavy cart the same acceleration as a light cart, you must push the heavy cart with...
questions.explain: F = ma: more mass needs more force for the same acceleration.

questions.q: A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward and the rocket moves upward. This is an example of...
options: Newton's third law - action and reaction forces
questions.explain: The action (gas pushed down) produces an equal, opposite reaction (rocket pushed up).

questions.q: When you swim, you push water backward and your body moves forward. The forward push on your body is...
options: the reaction force from the water
questions.explain: By Newton's third law, the water pushes back on you with an equal, opposite force.

questions.q: Why don't action-reaction forces cancel each other out?
questions.explain: Forces only cancel when they act on the SAME object; action-reaction pairs act on two objects.

questions.q: A book pushes down on a table with a force of 5 newtons. What is the reaction force?
options: The table pushes down on the floor with 5 newtons
Gravity pulls the book with 10 newtons
The table pushes up on the book with 5 newtons
questions.explain: Newton's third law: the table exerts an equal and opposite force on the book.

questions.q: A seatbelt protects you in a crash mainly because it...
options: applies a force that stops your body along with the car, overcoming your inertia
questions.explain: Without a belt, your body keeps moving forward (inertia) after the car stops.

questions.q: Which situation shows Newton's first law?
options: A ball falls faster and faster
A car speeds up when the driver presses the gas
A hockey puck slides across smooth ice and keeps going at nearly constant speed
questions.explain: With almost no friction, the puck continues in motion - Newton's first law.

questions.q: A 4-kilogram object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared. What net force is acting on it?
questions.explain: F = ma = 4 x 3 = 12 newtons.

questions.q: If the net force on an object doubles while its mass stays the same, its acceleration will...
questions.explain: a = F/m, so doubling F doubles the acceleration.

questions.q: Which term means: the tendency of an object to resist any change in its motion?
questions.explain: The term 'inertia' means the tendency of an object to resist any change in its motion.

questions.q: What does the term 'newton's first law' mean?
options: the overall force acting on an object after all individual forces are combined
forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction, resulting in no change in motion
a simple machine made of a flat, sloped surface, such as a ramp
the law stating that an object at rest or in motion stays that way unless an unbalanced force acts on it
questions.explain: 'Newton's first law' means the law stating that an object at rest or in motion stays that way unless an unbalanced force acts on it.

questions.q: What does the term 'newton's second law' mean?
options: the law stating that acceleration depends on the object's mass and the net force applied (F = ma)
a push or a pull exerted on an object
the law stating that an object at rest or in motion stays that way unless an unbalanced force acts on it
a simple machine made of a bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum
questions.explain: 'Newton's second law' means the law stating that acceleration depends on the object's mass and the net force applied (F = ma).

questions.q: What does the term 'newton's third law' mean?
options: a simple machine made of a bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum
a simple machine made of a grooved wheel with a rope or cable around it
the law stating that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force
a place or object used for comparison to determine whether an object is in motion
questions.explain: 'Newton's third law' means the law stating that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

questions.q: A net force accelerates a 2-kilogram object at 2 meters per second squared. What is the net force?
questions.explain: Newton's second law: F = ma = 2 x 2 = 4 newtons.

questions.q: A net force accelerates a 5-kilogram object at 3 meters per second squared. What is the net force?
questions.explain: Newton's second law: F = ma = 5 x 3 = 15 newtons.

questions.q: A car's velocity changes from 5 meters per second to 7 meters per second in 2 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration = (final - initial velocity) / time = (7 - 5) / 2 = 1 meters per second squared.

questions.q: A car's velocity changes from 0 meters per second to 6 meters per second in 2 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration = (final - initial velocity) / time = (6 - 0) / 2 = 3 meters per second squared.

rounds.title: Forces & Motion - Quest 3
rounds.desc: Newton's three laws of motion in everyday situations.

title: Forces & Motion - Quest 4
subject: Middle School Science
description: Boss quest: work, simple machines, and mechanical advantage.

questions.q: A ramp used to load a truck is an example of which simple machine?
questions.explain: A ramp is an inclined plane that spreads the lifting force over a longer distance.

questions.q: A knife blade is an example of which simple machine?
questions.explain: A wedge is two inclined planes joined to split or cut materials.

questions.q: The flagpole at school uses which simple machine to raise the flag?
questions.explain: A pulley changes the direction of the force used to lift the flag.

questions.q: A seesaw is an example of a...
questions.explain: A seesaw bar pivots on a fulcrum: a lever.

questions.q: The fixed point on which a lever pivots is called the...
questions.explain: Levers rotate around the fulcrum.

questions.q: A jar lid and a wood screw are examples of which simple machine?
options: screw - an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder
questions.explain: A screw's threads are an inclined plane wrapped in a spiral.

questions.q: A doorknob is an example of which simple machine?
questions.explain: The knob (wheel) turns a thinner rod (axle): a wheel and axle.

questions.q: In science, work is done on an object only when...
options: a force causes the object to move in the direction of the force
you push on something, even if it does not move
questions.explain: No movement in the force's direction means no work, however hard you push.

questions.q: You push against a brick wall with all your strength and it does not move. How much work did you do on the wall?
options: It depends on how tired you feel
Your full body weight in joules
questions.explain: Work = force x distance; with zero distance moved, work is zero.

questions.q: Simple machines make work easier, but they do NOT...
options: change the direction of a force
increase the force you can apply
reduce the total amount of work needed
questions.explain: Machines trade force and distance; ignoring friction, total work stays the same.

questions.q: A longer, gentler ramp requires ______ force to push a box to the same height, but the box travels a longer distance.
questions.explain: An inclined plane trades a smaller force over a longer distance.

questions.q: Adding more supporting ropes to a pulley system generally...
options: decreases the distance the load moves to zero
increases the mechanical advantage, so less effort force is needed
removes the need for any force
questions.explain: More rope segments share the load, multiplying the effort force.

questions.q: Which term means: the use of a force to move an object through a distance, measured in joules?
questions.explain: The term 'work' means the use of a force to move an object through a distance, measured in joules.

questions.q: Which term means: a device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force?
questions.explain: The term 'simple machine' means a device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force.

questions.q: Which term means: a simple machine made of a bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum?
questions.explain: The term 'lever' means a simple machine made of a bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum.

questions.q: What does the term 'mechanical advantage' mean?
options: the SI unit used to measure force
the tendency of an object to resist any change in its motion
the number of times a machine multiplies the input force
the law stating that an object at rest or in motion stays that way unless an unbalanced force acts on it
questions.explain: 'Mechanical advantage' means the number of times a machine multiplies the input force.

questions.q: A worker pushes a crate with a force of 20 newtons for a distance of 5 meters. How much work is done on the crate?
questions.explain: Work = force x distance = 20 x 5 = 100 joules.

questions.q: A worker pushes a crate with a force of 25 newtons for a distance of 5 meters. How much work is done on the crate?
questions.explain: Work = force x distance = 25 x 5 = 125 joules.

questions.q: A machine lets a worker lift a load of 100 newtons using an effort force of only 20 newtons. What is the machine's mechanical advantage?
questions.explain: Mechanical advantage = load force / effort force = 100 / 20 = 5.

questions.q: A machine lets a worker lift a load of 50 newtons using an effort force of only 10 newtons. What is the machine's mechanical advantage?
questions.explain: Mechanical advantage = load force / effort force = 50 / 10 = 5.

rounds.title: Forces & Motion - Quest 4
rounds.desc: Boss quest: work, simple machines, and mechanical advantage.

title: Energy, Heat & Waves - Quest 1
subject: Middle School Science
description: Kinetic and potential energy, transformations, and conservation.

questions.q: A battery stores energy in which form?
questions.explain: Batteries store energy in chemicals until a circuit releases it.

questions.q: A moving bicycle has mostly which form of energy?
questions.explain: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.

questions.q: At the top of a roller coaster hill, the cars have the most...
questions.explain: Height gives the cars stored gravitational potential energy.

questions.q: As the roller coaster dives down the hill, energy changes from...
options: kinetic energy to potential energy only
energy is created at the bottom
questions.explain: Falling converts stored potential energy into motion energy.

questions.q: In a flashlight, the main energy transformation is...
options: chemical energy -> electrical energy -> light energy (and some thermal energy)
questions.explain: Battery chemicals drive a current that the bulb turns into light.

questions.q: The law of conservation of energy states that energy...
options: cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed or transferred
questions.explain: Energy changes form but the total amount stays the same.

questions.q: A stretched rubber band has...
options: no energy until it is released
questions.explain: Stretching stores elastic potential energy in the band.

questions.q: If the speed of a moving object doubles, its kinetic energy...
options: increases by about four times, because kinetic energy depends on speed squared
questions.explain: KE = 1/2 mv^2, so doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.

questions.q: Which object has the greatest kinetic energy?
options: a truck moving at highway speed
a book on a high shelf
questions.explain: The moving truck combines large mass with high speed.

questions.q: Plants capture light energy and store it as...
questions.explain: Photosynthesis stores sunlight's energy in the bonds of glucose.

questions.q: When a ball rolls to a stop on a flat floor, its kinetic energy is mostly transformed into...
questions.explain: Friction converts the ball's motion energy into heat in the ball and floor.

questions.q: Fossil fuels store chemical energy that originally came from...
options: sunlight captured by ancient living things
questions.explain: Coal, oil, and gas formed from ancient organisms that stored solar energy.

questions.q: Which term means: the ability to do work or cause change?
questions.explain: The term 'energy' means the ability to do work or cause change.

questions.q: Which term means: the energy an object has because of its motion; it increases with mass and with speed?
questions.explain: The term 'kinetic energy' means the energy an object has because of its motion; it increases with mass and with speed.

questions.q: Which term means: stored energy an object has because of its position or condition?
questions.explain: The term 'potential energy' means stored energy an object has because of its position or condition.

questions.q: Which term means: the total kinetic energy of all the particles in a substance?
questions.explain: The term 'thermal energy' means the total kinetic energy of all the particles in a substance.

questions.q: An object with a mass of 2 kilograms moves at 2 meters per second. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = 1/2 x mass x speed^2)
questions.explain: KE = 1/2 x 2 x 2^2 = 4 joules.

questions.q: An object with a mass of 2 kilograms moves at 3 meters per second. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = 1/2 x mass x speed^2)
questions.explain: KE = 1/2 x 2 x 3^2 = 9 joules.

questions.q: A 3-kilogram book sits on a shelf 5 meters above the floor. Using g = 10 newtons per kilogram, what is its gravitational potential energy? (PE = mass x g x height)
questions.explain: PE = 3 x 10 x 5 = 150 joules.

questions.q: A 1-kilogram book sits on a shelf 10 meters above the floor. Using g = 10 newtons per kilogram, what is its gravitational potential energy? (PE = mass x g x height)
questions.explain: PE = 1 x 10 x 10 = 100 joules.

rounds.title: Energy, Heat & Waves - Quest 1
rounds.desc: Kinetic and potential energy, transformations, and conservation.

title: Energy, Heat & Waves - Quest 2
subject: Middle School Science
description: Conduction, convection, and radiation move heat from warm to cool.

questions.q: A metal spoon left in a pot of hot soup becomes hot at the handle end. This heat transfer is...
questions.explain: Heat travels through the metal by direct contact of particles: conduction.

questions.q: Warm air rising and cool air sinking to take its place creates which kind of heat transfer?
questions.explain: Fluid movement caused by density differences transfers heat by convection.

questions.q: The Sun warms the Earth across empty space by...
questions.explain: Electromagnetic radiation carries energy through the vacuum of space.

questions.q: Heat always flows spontaneously from...
options: a larger object to a smaller object
a cooler object to a warmer object
a warmer object to a cooler object
questions.explain: Thermal energy transfers from higher temperature to lower temperature.

questions.q: A foam cup keeps a cold drink cold mainly because foam is a good...
questions.explain: Foam traps air and slows conduction, keeping heat out.

questions.q: Why does a tile floor feel colder than a carpet at the same room temperature?
options: Tile is actually much colder than the carpet
Tile conducts heat away from your feet faster than carpet does
Your feet produce less heat on tile
questions.explain: Both are at room temperature, but tile is a better conductor, so it draws heat faster.

questions.q: Why do cooks use wooden or plastic handles on metal pans?
options: Wood makes the pan heat faster
Wood and plastic are insulators that stay cooler and protect hands
questions.explain: Insulating handles slow heat conduction from the hot pan.

questions.q: In a room heated by a radiator, the air near the ceiling becomes warm because...
options: heated air expands, becomes less dense, and rises by convection
heat travels downward through air by conduction
cold air rises above warm air
questions.explain: Warm, less-dense air rises, carrying thermal energy upward.

questions.q: Two metal blocks at 80 degrees Celsius and 20 degrees Celsius are pressed together. What happens over time?
options: Both blocks heat up to 80 degrees
Nothing, because solids cannot transfer heat
The cold block makes the hot block colder than 20 degrees
Heat flows from the hotter block to the cooler one until both reach the same temperature
questions.explain: Heat flows hot to cold until thermal equilibrium is reached.

questions.q: Which material is the best conductor of heat?
questions.explain: Metals like copper conduct heat far better than wood, foam, or rubber.

questions.q: Wearing a thick coat in winter keeps you warm because the coat...
options: stops your body from producing heat
traps air and slows the loss of your body heat
reflects your body heat back using mirrors
questions.explain: Coats insulate; your body is the heat source.

questions.q: Feeling the warmth of a campfire on your face while standing a meter away is mainly due to...
options: conduction through the air molecules only
questions.explain: Infrared radiation travels from the fire to your skin without needing contact.

questions.q: Which term means: the transfer of heat energy through direct contact between materials?
questions.explain: The term 'conduction' means the transfer of heat energy through direct contact between materials.

questions.q: Which term means: the transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid in currents?
questions.explain: The term 'convection' means the transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid in currents.

questions.q: Which term means: the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space?
questions.explain: The term 'radiation' means the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space.

questions.q: Which term means: a material that slows the transfer of heat or electricity?
questions.explain: The term 'insulator' means a material that slows the transfer of heat or electricity.

questions.q: Convert 0 degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.explain: Fahrenheit = (Celsius x 9/5) + 32, so 0 degrees Celsius = 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Convert 25 degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.explain: Fahrenheit = (Celsius x 9/5) + 32, so 25 degrees Celsius = 77 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Convert 86 degrees Fahrenheit to degrees Celsius.
questions.explain: Celsius = (Fahrenheit - 32) x 5/9, so 86 degrees Fahrenheit = 30 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Convert 212 degrees Fahrenheit to degrees Celsius.
questions.explain: Celsius = (Fahrenheit - 32) x 5/9, so 212 degrees Fahrenheit = 100 degrees Celsius.

rounds.title: Energy, Heat & Waves - Quest 2
rounds.desc: Conduction, convection, and radiation move heat from warm to cool.

title: Energy, Heat & Waves - Quest 3
subject: Middle School Science
description: Wave properties, sound, pitch, and echoes.

questions.q: Waves transfer ______ from one place to another without transferring matter.
questions.explain: A wave carries energy; the medium's particles vibrate in place.

questions.q: Sound waves CANNOT travel through...
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium; space is a vacuum, so sound cannot cross it.

questions.q: You see lightning before you hear the thunder from the same strike because...
options: thunder travels the long way around
light travels much faster than sound
questions.explain: Light reaches you almost instantly; sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometer.

questions.q: The pitch of a sound is determined by its...
options: frequency - higher frequency means higher pitch
questions.explain: Pitch rises with frequency.

questions.q: A louder sound has waves with a greater...
questions.explain: Amplitude relates to a wave's energy: louder sounds and brighter lights have larger amplitudes.

questions.q: In a longitudinal sound wave, the particles of the medium...
options: travel with the wave to the listener
vibrate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels, forming compressions
move in circles around the wave
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions.

questions.q: The highest point of a transverse wave is called the...
questions.explain: The crest is the top of the wave; the trough is the bottom.

questions.q: An echo is produced when sound waves...
options: reflect off a distant surface and return
questions.explain: Reflected sound returning to your ears is an echo.

questions.q: Ships use sonar to find the depth of the ocean by...
